# Introduction

Cluster randomized trials (CRTs) randomize intact groups, such as clinics, schools, or geographic areas, rather than individuals. They are the standard design when an intervention is delivered at the group level or when individual randomization would create unacceptable contamination between arms [@donner_design_2000; @hayes_cluster_2017]. Standard CRT analysis relies on the no-interference component of the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA): a cluster's outcome must not depend on which other clusters were assigned to treatment [@Rubin1986]. This assumption comes from the theory of individually randomized trials. It can fail once clusters are spatially arranged, as can the weaker assumption of partial interference, under which outcomes may depend on assignments within prespecified groups but not across them [@hudgens_toward_2008]. Tobler's first law of geography states that "everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things" [@tobler_computer_1970]. By this principle, an intervention delivered in one location can plausibly influence outcomes in adjacent locations through shared populations, service networks, information diffusion, or environmental pathways. Documented examples of spatial spillover come from public health and development economics. In a trial of insecticide-treated bed nets in northern Ghana, child mortality was lower in control villages close to treated villages than in control villages farther away [@binka_impact_1998]. A school-based deworming trial in Kenya found health and attendance benefits among untreated children near treated schools [@miguel_worms_2004]. When control clusters benefit from nearby treatment, an unadjusted comparison of treated and control clusters may understate the direct effect. How much contamination occurs can depend on the spatial arrangement of the two arms, not only on the number of clusters allocated to each.

## The design-stage gap in the spatial interference literature

Methods for spatial interference in CRTs have concentrated on correction at the analysis stage (Chapter 1). Spatial autocorrelation statistics such as Moran's $I$ [@moran_interpretation_1948] detect residual spatial dependence once outcomes have been observed. Spatial regression models, such as the spatial lag model [@lesage_introduction_2009] estimated by maximum likelihood [@ord_estimation_1975] and implemented in software [@bivand_r_2022], allow an analyst to separate a direct treatment effect from a spillover effect after the fact. In their systematic review of spatial analysis methods for cluster randomized trials, Jarvis and colleagues placed trials that used spatial separation or buffers outside the primary review of statistical methods [@jarvis_spatial_2017]. The literature therefore offers much more guidance on analyzing spatial effects than on how the choice of treatment assignment itself, made before any data are collected, might reduce the problem.

Design-stage tools do exist, but they were largely developed for a different purpose. Restricted and covariate-constrained randomization address the baseline imbalance that a limited number of clusters can produce [@raab_balance_2001; @moulton_covariatebased_2004]. Crisp and colleagues noted that their extension, which selects clusters from a larger eligible set, also increases spatial dispersion among the selected clusters [@crisp_covariate-constrained_2023]. Their dispersion criterion concerns which clusters are selected, not how they are assigned to arms. Balancing a covariate across arms also does not by itself determine whether treated and control clusters are spatially interspersed in a way that induces contamination. Other work addresses the problem studied here more directly. Randomized saturation designs assign different fractions of units treated to different groups so that direct and spillover effects can be jointly identified [@baird_optimal_2018]. Another approach selects whole clusters for inclusion or exclusion in place of a "fried-egg" design that omits each cluster's outer area from analysis [@mccann_spatial_2018]. Recent theoretical work develops designs under spatial, network and cross-cluster interference and spatio-temporal heterogeneity [@leung_rateoptimal_2022; @cai_independentset_2023; @leung_clusterrandomized_2025; @watson_design_2025]. This chapter complements that work with a simulation comparison of concrete assignment strategies that a trial team could implement, under heterogeneous baseline incidence and a range of spatial dependence and spillover conditions.

## Extending Chapter 2

Chapter 2 examined block-stratified allocation as a practical way to obtain reasonably good estimation while limiting poor-allocation risk in the settings it studied. This chapter evaluates both criteria across a broader set of designs under heterogeneous incidence. We retain Chapter 2's simple random assignment benchmark and strict alternating allocation, called Checkerboard here, while adding incidence balancing, targeting, saturation and isolation strategies. The grid comparison increases the number of clusters from 8--12 to 100, considers queen as well as rook neighbors, and includes heterogeneous baseline incidence in the outcome model. These changes extend the design question, so the results are not a direct numerical replication of Chapter 2. In Chapter 2, $\beta$ denotes the intervention effect. Here that effect is $\tau$, and $\beta$ denotes the coefficient of the incidence covariate. The observed-incidence application later in the chapter uses the North Carolina (NC) community college geography and a continuous education outcome, without assuming that historical sudden unexpected death (SUD) incidence predicts baseline education performance.

## Aims and outline

This chapter has three aims: (1) compare assignment designs by mean squared error (MSE), bias and confidence interval coverage, (2) assess how conclusions depend on incidence heterogeneity, spatial dependence, spillover regime and treatment-effect magnitude, and (3) assess both average accuracy and allocation-specific downside for planning a SUD-prevention education pilot on an observed North Carolina geography. The detailed grid results present six designs, and the appendix documents the two related variants. A main-text benchmark includes all eight strategies and simple random sampling (SRS). The completed application evaluates all nine strategies separately for each observed planning year. The application simulates outcomes and assignments and does not report outcomes from an implemented intervention.

The Methods set out the outcome model, the baseline incidence mechanisms used on the grid, the treatment assignment designs, and the estimator and performance criteria, and then describe the grid simulation. The Results compare the designs on the 100-cluster grid, overall and by incidence configuration, spatial dependence and spillover regime, and then compare each design with SRS. Later subsections report how the comparison changes with the treatment effect, across parameter settings and across allocations, and the last two give sensitivity analyses for rook contiguity and for a model without the spillover term. The application then evaluates the same designs on the observed NC geography, including participation and power. The Discussion draws out implications for trial design and for the SUD education pilot.

# Methods

## Spatial structure, outcome model and estimand

The grid study uses a $10\times10$ regular grid of 100 clusters, and the application uses 58 community college service areas in North Carolina. In both, clusters are linked under one of two definitions of adjacency. Under queen contiguity, two clusters are neighbors if they share an edge or a corner. Under rook contiguity, they must share an edge. Queen contiguity is the primary analysis in this chapter. Rook contiguity is a sensitivity analysis and the case that continues Chapter 2, whose grids used rook neighbors. For each definition, the binary adjacency matrix was row-standardized to form the spatial weights matrix $W$. The product $WZ$ then gives, for each cluster, the proportion of its neighbors that are treated, and $WY$ gives the average outcome among its neighbors. Row-standardization expresses each cluster's spillover exposure as an average over its own neighborhood rather than a raw sum, which would otherwise depend on how many neighbors the cluster has. Within a scenario, the same neighbor type defines $W$ in the outcome model, in the Isolation Buffer design, and in the fitted model.

Cluster-level outcomes $Y$ were generated from a spatial lag model with a spillover term,
\begin{equation}
Y = (I - \rho W)^{-1}\left[\tau Z + S(Z) + \beta X + \epsilon\right], \qquad \epsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2 I),
\label{eq:outcome}
\end{equation}
where $Z \in \{0,1\}^{N}$ is the treatment assignment of the $N$ clusters produced by the design under evaluation, $\tau$ is the direct treatment effect of interest, $S(Z)$ is the spillover term defined in Equation \ref{eq:spillover}, $\rho$ is the spatial autoregressive coefficient governing dependence in the outcome beyond that induced by treatment and spillover, $X$ is the baseline incidence covariate with coefficient $\beta = 1$, and $\sigma = 1$. The spatial multiplier $(I-\rho W)^{-1}$ propagates each cluster's shocks through the network of neighbors. The effect $\tau$ is the coefficient of a cluster's own treatment before spatial propagation, not an average total effect after applying $(I-\rho W)^{-1}$. When $\rho = 0$ the multiplier is the identity and the model is a linear regression with independent errors, $Y = \tau Z + S(Z) + \beta X + \epsilon$, in which spatial structure enters only through the spillover term. Larger values of $\rho$ induce progressively stronger spatial clustering in the outcome. Setting $\beta = 1$ makes incidence prognostic, so higher-incidence clusters have higher baseline outcomes. This is the harder case for designs that use incidence, because treatment can then line up with baseline risk. Investigators can choose $\beta$ to suit their own outcome. The application's education outcome is not expected to depend on SUD incidence, so its primary analysis uses $\beta = 0$.

We evaluated two spillover regimes,
\begin{equation}
S(Z) = \gamma\, WZ \quad \text{(both arms)}, \qquad S(Z) = \gamma\, WZ \circ (1 - Z) \quad \text{(control only)},
\label{eq:spillover}
\end{equation}
where $\circ$ denotes the elementwise product. Under the control-only regime, only untreated clusters respond to the treatment status of their neighbors. This is classical contamination: an untreated cluster's outcome rises with the share of its neighbors that are treated. Under the both-arms regime, every cluster responds to its neighbors' treatment regardless of its own assignment, so neighboring treatment adds to a treated cluster's own effect.

## Heterogeneous baseline incidence

Chapter 2 assumed a spatially uniform baseline outcome risk. Cluster-level health outcomes typically vary across space, and the designs studied here differ in whether and how they use that variation. We generated the baseline incidence covariate $X$, with values in $(0, 1)$, under three mechanisms. Under the independent (iid) mechanism, each $X_i$ is drawn from a Uniform$(0,1)$ distribution, with no spatial structure. The spatially autocorrelated mechanism sets $X = \Phi\{(I - \rho_X W_Q)^{-1} u\}$, where $u \sim N(0, I)$, $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function applied elementwise, $W_Q$ is the queen weights matrix, and $\rho_X \in \{0.20, 0.50\}$. Under the Poisson mechanism, a spatially autocorrelated log-rate surface, $\log \lambda = \log(35/100{,}000) + (I - \rho_X W_Q)^{-1} u$ with $\rho_X \in \{0.20, 0.50\}$, generates cluster death counts $C_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i P)$, with an equal population of $P = 100{,}000$ in every cluster, so that a cluster at the base rate expects 35 deaths. The observed rates $C_i / P$ are then rank-normalized to $X_i = (r_i - 0.5)/N$, where $r_i$ is the rank of cluster $i$'s rate among the $N = 100$ clusters and tied rates share their average rank. Ties remain at this population size: the Poisson surfaces used here have between 60 and 76 distinct values among the 100 clusters. The base rate of 35 per 100,000 was chosen to represent published SUD incidence. It lies between the SUD incidence rates that Mirzaei and colleagues estimated for US men (49.3 per 100,000) and women (21.7 per 100,000) aged 20--64, close to their average [@mirzaei_years_2019]. It is not the observed rate of the county data described in the Application section, which come from a different source, age range, period, and case definition. The incidence filters always use the queen weights $W_Q$, whichever neighbor type the scenario uses, so the incidence surfaces are identical under rook and queen contiguity. The iid mechanism and the two strengths of each of the other two mechanisms give five incidence configurations.

For each configuration we generated $K = 10$ incidence surfaces, $X_1, \dots, X_{10}$, each from its own seed. The same ten surfaces are used by every scenario in that configuration, across neighbor types, outcome-model parameters, designs, and values of $\tau$. The design draws and the outcome noise are shared more selectively, as described under Simulation design, resampling, and metrics. Each design is applied to the surface that generates the outcome: assignments for surface $k$ are drawn from $X_k$, and the outcome and the fitted model for those assignments use $X_k$ as well. We call this the matched-surface assumption: the incidence observed when a trial is planned is the incidence that drives its outcome. The target of each scenario is performance averaged over incidence surfaces; for example, $\text{MSE} = E_X E_{Z \mid X} E_\epsilon[(\hat\tau - \tau)^2]$, with $X$ drawn from the configuration's generator, $Z$ from the design given $X$, and $\epsilon \sim N(0, I)$. Bias, coverage, and power are defined in the same way.

## Treatment assignment designs

We implemented eight treatment assignment designs and present six of them as the primary comparison set in this chapter. The other two, Saturation Quadrants and Balanced Halves, each share the mechanism of a retained design. In a comparison of the eight designs and SRS at $\tau = 1$, neither could be distinguished from its counterpart under either neighbor type (Appendix \ref{app:eight-design}). Saturation Quadrants assigns the saturations 20\%, 40\%, 60\%, and 80\% to the four $5\times5$ quadrants of the grid in random order, without reference to incidence. Its retained counterpart, Incidence-Guided Saturation, assigns the higher saturations to the quadrants with higher mean incidence (Table \ref{tab:designs}). On the NC map, both designs use four fixed geographic regions in place of the quadrants. Balanced Halves divides clusters into two halves by incidence rank and treats 25 at random in each. Its retained counterpart, Balanced Quartiles, uses four strata. In each pair the excluded design had the marginally lower mean squared error or average rank under at least one neighbor type, so the choice of representative does not rest on performance. The two saturation designs performed similarly, so incidence guidance matches the accuracy of Saturation Quadrants while directing the highest treatment saturations to the quadrants or regions with the highest incidence. How much treatment it redirects depends on how much incidence differs between regions (see Application). The accuracy advantage of both designs over SRS, which arises under control-only spillover (see Comparison with simple random sampling), comes from the saturation structure they share. Both variants are included in the full benchmark with SRS and in the application.

Table \ref{tab:designs} describes the six retained designs, and Figure \ref{fig:design-samples} shows one assignment from each, and from SRS, on a single illustrative incidence surface. Checkerboard is the strict block-stratified allocation of Chapter 2, in which no two rook neighbors share an arm. Chapter 2's Block Stratified Sampling design also admitted relaxed allocations on its $3\times3$ grid, where the arms cannot be balanced. On its $2\times4$ and $3\times4$ grids, as on the $10\times10$ grid here, the strict allocations are the two checkerboard patterns. We use the two names interchangeably for this allocation and use Checkerboard in the rest of this chapter. Checkerboard is the only deterministic design: it gives the same assignment in every draw, although each of its fits still receives its own outcome noise. Every other design was drawn independently 25 times for each incidence surface. Designs that rank clusters by incidence break ties at random, afresh for each draw. High Incidence Focus is random only through that tie-breaking. Under the iid and spatial mechanisms, incidence values are distinct, so it gives the same assignment in all 25 draws on a surface, and that assignment changes only from one surface to the next. Isolation Buffer builds its assignment from the neighbor type of the scenario, and it treats 38 clusters on average under rook contiguity and 21 under queen contiguity. Every other design treats exactly 50.

## Estimation and performance criteria

We estimated $\tau$ with two maximum likelihood spatial lag models, both fit to every simulated outcome and both including an intercept. The primary, oracle model has the spatial lag $\rho WY$ and the covariates $Z$, $\text{Spill} = S(Z)$, and $X_k$, so it matches the outcome model in Equation \ref{eq:outcome}, including the true regime-specific spillover covariate from Equation \ref{eq:spillover}. The oracle model assumes that the analyst knows the form of the spillover mechanism and has the exact exposure term, so its results are a best case for each design. We return to this assumption as a limitation. The non-oracle model, a sensitivity analysis, has the covariates $Z$ and $X_k$ only and omits the spillover term. Both models are fit to the same outcomes.

We fit both models with our own implementation of the maximum likelihood estimator of the spatial lag model [@bivand_comparing_2015], the same estimator that the `lagsarlm` function of the R package `spatialreg` computes with `method = "eigen"`. It maximizes the concentrated log-likelihood over $\rho$, computing the log-determinant from the eigenvalues of $W$ [@ord_estimation_1975], estimates the remaining coefficients by least squares given $\hat\rho$, and computes standard errors from the analytic information matrix. On 5,120 validation fits it agreed with `lagsarlm` to within $9.7\times10^{-8}$ in $\hat\tau$ and to a relative difference of $1.1\times10^{-8}$ in its standard error, at roughly 1\% of the computing time. As a further check, we refit a 1\% sample of the full simulation with `lagsarlm` itself. Confidence intervals are 95\% intervals with a $t$ reference distribution and a degrees-of-freedom-corrected standard error, $\hat\tau \pm t_{0.975,\,N-p}\,\widehat{\text{SE}}\sqrt{N/(N-p)}$. Here $\widehat{\text{SE}}$ is the estimated standard error, $N = 100$ is the number of clusters and $p$ is the number of regression coefficients plus $\rho$: 5 for the oracle model, and 4 for the non-oracle model and for rook Checkerboard, whose aliased spillover column is dropped. The application uses the same interval. The 95\% Wald interval, $\hat\tau \pm 1.96\,\widehat{\text{SE}}$, covered about one percentage point less for every design.

Checkerboard illustrates why interspersion alone cannot guarantee precision. Under rook contiguity on the rectangular grid, $WZ=1-Z$, so treatment and spillover cannot be separately identified, and the fitted coefficient on treatment estimates $\tau-\gamma$. Under queen contiguity, treatment is identified but control-only spillover is weakly separated from treatment. We retain Checkerboard in the main design comparison and flag aliased estimates. Exact matrix identities, boundary information and the rare Isolation Buffer aliases are detailed in Appendix \ref{app:technical}. These diagnostics apply only to the two models fitted here.

Because a trial realizes only one allocation, we judge each design on two criteria: the error of the estimate averaged over the allocations the design can produce, and how that error varies from one allocation to another. The risk of assignment $a$ is the conditional MSE $m(a)=E_\epsilon[(\hat\tau-\tau)^2\mid a,X]$. We estimated it by simulating repeated outcomes for each sampled assignment and then compared its distribution across assignments. This distribution across assignments differs from the distribution of squared errors in a single allocation and from MSE across parameter scenarios.

A design's MSE is the average of $m(a)$ over its assignments and, in the grid study, over incidence surfaces. Bias, coverage of the 95\% interval and power are averaged over assignments and outcome noise in the same way. We summarize the variation across assignments by the estimated 90th percentile of $m(a)$ among sampled assignments and by the worst-decile mean, the mean of $m(a)$ over the worst 10\% of sampled assignments.

## Simulation design, resampling, and metrics

We tested four values of the outcome spatial dependence, $\rho \in \{0, 0.01, 0.20, 0.50\}$, four spillover magnitudes, $\gamma \in \{0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8\}$, and five magnitudes of the direct effect, $\tau \in \{0.8, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0\}$, with $\tau = 1$ as the primary scenario throughout. The full simulation crossed five values of $\tau$, five incidence configurations, two neighbor types, four values of $\rho$, four values of $\gamma$, two spillover regimes, and eight designs, for $5 \times 5 \times 2 \times 4 \times 4 \times 2 \times 8 = 12{,}800$ scenarios, of which the six designs reported in this chapter account for 9,600. We call a combination of incidence configuration, neighbor type, $\rho$, $\gamma$, and spillover regime a block. This gives $5 \times 2 \times 4 \times 4 \times 2 = 320$ blocks, 160 for each neighbor type. At the primary scenario, $\tau = 1$, the six designs give 1,920 scenarios, and every block contains all six.

Within each scenario, we drew $J = 25$ assignments from each of the $K = 10$ incidence surfaces, for 250 fits per scenario. Every fit had its own noise vector, so that fit $(k, j)$ has outcome $Y_{kj} = (I - \rho W)^{-1}[\tau Z_{kj} + S(Z_{kj}) + \beta X_k + \epsilon_{kj}]$. Checkerboard's 250 fits share one assignment but have 250 distinct noise vectors. The ten surfaces are independent, so the surface is the primary sampling unit. Each estimator was fit 3.2 million times. SRS assigns exactly 50 of the 100 clusters to treatment by complete randomization, ignoring incidence and geography. We ran it afterward with the same matched surfaces, noise keys and 250-fit structure, which brought the complete benchmark to 14,400 scenarios and 3.6 million fits per estimator. Adding SRS left the original eight-design results unchanged.

Every random draw was seeded from a key that names the draw, so the results do not depend on the order in which scenarios are run. The keys also give common random numbers. Within a block, all designs share the same noise vectors and incidence surfaces, the five values of $\tau$ reuse the same assignments and noise, and the oracle and non-oracle models are fit to the same outcomes. Blocks within an incidence configuration share its ten surfaces.

For each scenario and estimator, we computed bias, the standard deviation (SD) of $\hat\tau$, MSE, coverage of the 95\% interval, and power, the fraction of fits whose interval lies above zero (a one-sided test of $\tau = 0$ at level 0.025). For both estimators, every one of the 250 fits in every scenario was valid, with a finite estimate and standard error, and the fitting routine raised no warning other than the aliasing flags described above. Each metric is estimated from a finite number of simulated datasets, so it carries Monte Carlo error. Its Monte Carlo standard error measures this uncertainty and shrinks as more datasets are simulated [@morris_using_2019]. Monte Carlo standard errors come from the surface-level metrics: with $m_k$ a metric computed on the 25 fits from surface $k$, $\text{SE}(m) = \text{sd}(m_1, \dots, m_{10})/\sqrt{10}$, and, for metrics pooled over the five incidence configurations, from the 50 independent configuration-by-surface means. Appendix \ref{app:mechanics} gives the parameter grid, the seed keys, and the exact formulas for the metrics, their standard errors, and paired differences between designs.

We compared designs within each neighbor type with a Friedman rank-sum test on scenario MSE [@friedman_use_1937], treating the 160 blocks as repeated measures across the six designs and SRS. SRS is the usual default for a cluster randomized trial, so it enters every test as a seventh member and each design is compared with it as well as with the other designs. At $\tau = 1$ we followed the Friedman test with Nemenyi post-hoc comparisons [@nemenyi_distributionfree_1963; @demsar_statistical_2006] and paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests [@wilcoxon_individual_1945] with Holm's adjustment for multiple comparisons [@holm_simple_1979] for all 21 pairs. We repeated the Friedman test at each other value of $\tau$. Blocks within an incidence configuration share their surfaces, so these tests treat dependent blocks as independent, which overstates the information about variation from surface to surface. We therefore also ran paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with $t_{49}$ intervals for the mean difference, over 50 independent units, the 5 configurations times 10 surfaces. Each unit's MSE was averaged over that surface's blocks. These tests compared each pair of designs adjacent in the mean-MSE order, and each design with SRS within each spillover regime, with Holm's adjustment over the eight designs compared with SRS. Because the values of $\tau$ share assignments and noise, Friedman tests at different values of $\tau$ are not independent confirmations of one another.

We also ran an allocation-risk study with queen weights, $\tau=1$, all ten surfaces from each incidence configuration and the extreme combinations of $\rho$ and $\gamma$, $\rho\in\{0,0.5\}$ and $\gamma\in\{0.5,0.8\}$. The study used 100 assignment draws for each randomized design and 100 simulated outcomes per distinct assignment. As a precision check, one setting (surface 1, $\rho=0.5$, $\gamma=0.8$) was refined to 400 outcomes on the same assignments. A design with only one possible assignment received its own outcome replication.

We report results separately for each neighbor type, with queen contiguity primary, and never average a number over the two. Unless stated otherwise, every number in the Results is pooled over the five incidence configurations, and every table and figure caption states whether it pools the configurations or shows them separately. We report the ranking within each configuration separately and show the split wherever a conclusion changes.

# Results

## Design performance under queen contiguity

At the primary scenario, $\tau = 1$, under queen contiguity and pooled over the five incidence configurations, Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lowest mean squared error (MSE = 0.091), followed by Balanced Quartiles (0.131), Isolation Buffer (0.160), High Incidence Focus (0.245), $2\times2$ Blocking (0.319), and Checkerboard (1.087) (Table \ref{tab:performance}, Figure \ref{fig:mse}). Coverage of the 95\% intervals was between 0.946 and 0.950 for all six designs (Figure \ref{fig:coverage} in Appendix \ref{app:rook-figures}). Power to reject $\tau = 0$ was 0.921 for Incidence-Guided Saturation, 0.814 for Balanced Quartiles, 0.706 for Isolation Buffer, 0.629 for $2\times2$ Blocking, 0.582 for High Incidence Focus, and 0.538 for Checkerboard.

The Friedman test rejected equal MSE ranks across the six designs and SRS under queen contiguity at $\tau = 1$ ($\chi^2 = 560.33$, $\text{df} = 6$, 160 blocks, $p < 2.2\times10^{-16}$). Nemenyi comparisons (critical difference 0.712) separated 17 of the 21 pairs. Incidence-Guided Saturation ranked significantly better than every other design and than SRS ($p = 0.011$). SRS and Balanced Quartiles, whose average ranks were 2.60 and 2.69, could not be distinguished from each other ($p = 1.00$), and both ranked significantly better than the remaining four designs. The other three pairs not separated all lay among the bottom three designs. Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank tests separated 20 of the 21 pairs, all except Balanced Quartiles against SRS ($p = 0.15$). Because blocks within an incidence configuration share their ten surfaces, we also compared each pair of designs adjacent in the mean-MSE order over the 50 independent configuration-by-surface units. Every adjacent pair differed significantly (Wilcoxon $p \le 4.9\times10^{-9}$), and the better design had the lower MSE in all 50 units for every pair except High Incidence Focus against $2\times2$ Blocking (48 of 50). Appendix \ref{app:supp-comparisons} gives the pairwise results and the critical-difference diagrams.

The bottom three designs were ordered differently by average rank and by mean MSE: by mean MSE, High Incidence Focus (0.245), $2\times2$ Blocking (0.319), and Checkerboard (1.087). By average rank, the order was $2\times2$ Blocking (5.24), Checkerboard (5.74), and High Incidence Focus (5.76). Both reversals arise because the MSEs of $2\times2$ Blocking and Checkerboard depended strongly on the spillover regime. Each had a lower MSE than High Incidence Focus in all 80 both-arms blocks (mean MSE 0.062 for each, against 0.162) and a higher MSE in all 80 control-only blocks (0.576 and 2.111, against 0.329). Average rank counts each block once, so their wins under the both-arms regime offset their losses under the control-only regime. Mean MSE weights those losses by their size. The surface-level comparison, which averages each unit over both regimes, also separated High Incidence Focus from $2\times2$ Blocking.

## Incidence configuration, spatial dependence and spillover magnitude

Table \ref{tab:by-config} gives each design's MSE within each of the five incidence configurations. Under queen contiguity, the mean-MSE order within every configuration was the same as the pooled order: Incidence-Guided Saturation, Balanced Quartiles, Isolation Buffer, High Incidence Focus, $2\times2$ Blocking, and Checkerboard. The configuration changed each design's MSE only slightly: in this order, each design's highest MSE across the five configurations was lower than the next design's lowest. Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lowest MSE in 18 to 21 of the 32 blocks in each configuration. Coverage did not depend on the configuration either: within each configuration, every design's coverage, averaged over its 32 scenarios, was between 0.941 and 0.952. The mechanism that generated the incidence surface therefore did not change the ranking. The same held for High Incidence Focus, the design that uses the incidence ranks most directly: its MSE was no higher under the two Poisson configurations than under the iid and spatial configurations.

Under queen contiguity, neither the strength of spatial dependence in the outcome nor the spillover magnitude changed the ranking. Across $\rho \in \{0, 0.01, 0.20, 0.50\}$, no design's MSE changed by more than 0.02. Across $\gamma \in \{0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8\}$, the MSE of every design except Checkerboard also varied by less than 0.02, and Checkerboard's varied between 1.052 and 1.108 with no trend in $\gamma$ (Tables \ref{tab:rho} and \ref{tab:gamma} in Appendix \ref{app:sensitivity-tables}). Under rook contiguity, $\gamma$ mattered for Checkerboard alone, for the reason given in the rook results below.

## Spillover regime

The spillover regime was the one factor that changed the queen ranking (Table \ref{tab:regime}, Figure \ref{fig:mse}). Under the both-arms regime, Balanced Quartiles had the lowest MSE (0.042), followed by Incidence-Guided Saturation (0.046), $2\times2$ Blocking (0.062), Checkerboard (0.062), Isolation Buffer (0.161), and High Incidence Focus (0.162). Under the control-only regime, the order was Incidence-Guided Saturation (0.135), Isolation Buffer (0.159), Balanced Quartiles (0.219), High Incidence Focus (0.329), $2\times2$ Blocking (0.576), and Checkerboard (2.111). At larger values of $\tau$, Isolation Buffer matched or passed Incidence-Guided Saturation under this regime (see Stability across treatment effect sizes). For Isolation Buffer, no treated cluster has a treated neighbor, so $WZ = 0$ at every treated cluster and $WZ \circ (1 - Z) = WZ$. The two regimes in Equation \ref{eq:spillover} therefore define the same outcome model, and so the same expected MSE. The observed values, 0.161 and 0.159, differ only by Monte Carlo error because the two regimes use separate draws. Every other design had a higher MSE under the control-only regime. The increase was largest for Checkerboard and $2\times2$ Blocking, which went from close to the best designs under the both-arms regime to the two worst under the control-only regime. Among the six detailed designs, Incidence-Guided Saturation was first or second under both regimes, at this and every other value of $\tau$. In the full benchmark that includes SRS (Table \ref{tab:grid-srs}), its both-arms MSE was 8\% above that of SRS, a small but statistically detectable difference (Figure \ref{fig:vs-srs}). Its stable rank across regimes matters because a trial team may not know in advance which regime applies.

The increase under the control-only regime was variance, not bias. The oracle model includes the true regime-specific spillover covariate, so it has no omitted-variable bias. At $\tau = 1$, in every combination of design and regime under queen contiguity, the absolute bias was at most 0.048 and squared bias, averaged over scenarios, was at most 2.2\% of MSE. Checkerboard showed the mechanism most clearly: under the control-only regime its spillover covariate is a linear combination of the intercept and $Z$ at every interior cluster, so only the boundary clusters separate the spillover effect from the treatment effect (Methods). Checkerboard's MSE rose from 0.062 under the both-arms regime to 2.111 under the control-only regime, while its bias stayed near zero (0.004) and its coverage stayed at 0.951: its intervals widened with its variance. Its pooled MSE of 1.087 was almost entirely variance: squared bias, averaged over scenarios, was 0.0045, less than 0.5\% of MSE. Figure \ref{fig:biasvar} in Appendix \ref{app:rook-figures} shows the decomposition for the Poisson configuration with $\rho_X = 0.20$. $2\times2$ Blocking showed the same pattern on a smaller scale, with MSE rising from 0.062 to 0.576 and a bias of 0.016 under the control-only regime.

## Comparison with simple random sampling

At $\tau=1$ under queen contiguity, pooled over the five incidence configurations and all spatial and spillover settings, Incidence-Guided Saturation had mean MSE 0.0907 against 0.1285 for SRS, and Saturation Quadrants had 0.0900. Table \ref{tab:grid-srs} separates the regimes and includes all eight strategies. Figure \ref{fig:grid-srs} shows the six detailed designs and SRS with the five incidence configurations kept separate. Within each regime the configurations lie close together for every design, whereas the regime changes how each design compares with SRS. Incidence-Guided Saturation's MSE was 0.631 times that of SRS under control-only spillover and 1.083 times under both arms. SRS, Balanced Quartiles and Balanced Halves had similar both-arms accuracy. Small mean differences do not establish equivalence. Pooling over the regimes also hides how the design guidance differs between them.

Figure \ref{fig:vs-srs} tests each design against SRS within each regime, over the 50 independent configuration-by-surface units. Under control-only spillover, Incidence-Guided Saturation had 36.9\% lower MSE than SRS (95\% interval 34.5\% to 39.2\% lower), Saturation Quadrants 36.7\% lower and Isolation Buffer 25.7\% lower, each in all 50 units (Holm-adjusted $p = 6.2\times10^{-9}$). Under both-arms spillover, Incidence-Guided Saturation had 8.3\% higher MSE than SRS (5.6\% to 11.0\% higher; $p = 6.1\times10^{-6}$) and Saturation Quadrants 4.3\% higher ($p = 0.017$). Balanced Quartiles and Balanced Halves did not differ significantly from SRS under either regime. The remaining designs had significantly higher MSE than SRS under both-arms spillover, as did High Incidence Focus, $2\times2$ Blocking and Checkerboard under control-only spillover. The advantage of the saturation designs over SRS is therefore specific to control-only spillover, and under queen contiguity their small both-arms disadvantage is statistically detectable. Under rook contiguity the saturation designs had 23\% to 24\% lower control-only MSE than SRS and 3\% to 5\% higher both-arms MSE, significant for Incidence-Guided Saturation ($p = 0.0075$) but not for Saturation Quadrants ($p = 0.15$). Isolation Buffer's control-only MSE under rook contiguity was 5.8\% higher than that of SRS.

## Stability across treatment effect sizes

Under queen contiguity, the order by average within-block rank and the order by mean MSE were each the same at every $\tau \in \{0.8, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0\}$. The two orders differ from each other in the bottom three designs (see Design performance under queen contiguity; Figure \ref{fig:tau-mse}a shows mean MSE). With SRS included, the order by average rank placed SRS second at every value of $\tau$, and the Friedman statistic was 564.09, 560.33, 540.92, 526.55, and 497.55 at these five values ($p < 2.2\times10^{-16}$ at each). Under rook contiguity the order was also stable (Figure \ref{fig:tau-mse}b). By average rank among the six designs and SRS, it was the same at every value of $\tau$, with SRS third behind Incidence-Guided Saturation and Balanced Quartiles. By mean MSE, the close pair of $2\times2$ Blocking and Isolation Buffer traded places, with Isolation Buffer ahead only at $\tau = 3$. The five values of $\tau$ share their assignments and noise, so these five comparisons are not independent confirmations of one another. They show only that, under queen contiguity, the order did not change across the five values of $\tau$ we tested, given the same draws.

```

Within that stable order, the gap in MSE between Incidence-Guided Saturation and Balanced Quartiles under queen contiguity stayed between 0.037 and 0.041, and Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lower MSE of the two in 101 to 103 of the 160 blocks at every value of $\tau$. Isolation Buffer closed the gap instead: its MSE stayed at 0.160 at every value of $\tau$, while that of Incidence-Guided Saturation rose from 0.088 to 0.115 and that of Balanced Quartiles from 0.130 to 0.152. Isolation Buffer's gain came under the control-only regime, where the mean MSE of Incidence-Guided Saturation rose from 0.131 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.182 at $\tau = 3$, while that of Isolation Buffer stayed between 0.159 and 0.160. At $\tau = 2$ the two were level (0.1596 for Isolation Buffer against 0.1604), and at $\tau = 3$ Isolation Buffer had the lower control-only MSE (0.160 against 0.182). At $\tau = 2$ and $\tau = 3$, Isolation Buffer also had the lower worst case across all 160 blocks (0.207 against 0.210, and 0.208 against 0.238). Incidence-Guided Saturation remained second under the control-only regime at those two values, second to Balanced Quartiles under the both-arms regime at every value of $\tau$, and lowest in pooled MSE at every value of $\tau$. The rise in its MSE was mostly variance: its mean bias grew from 0.029 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.047 at $\tau = 3$, but squared bias stayed at or below 3.0\% of its MSE. Appendix \ref{app:technical-notes} traces both rises to a term of the estimation error that grows with $\tau$ when treated clusters have treated neighbors, and gives the block-level detail.

Under rook contiguity, Incidence-Guided Saturation kept the lowest control-only MSE at every value of $\tau$, although its margin over Isolation Buffer narrowed, from 0.095 against 0.134 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.131 against 0.136 at $\tau = 3$.

Except for Checkerboard under rook contiguity, coverage stayed close to 0.95 at every value of $\tau$: between 0.946 and 0.950 for every design under queen contiguity, and between 0.947 and 0.952 for every other design under rook contiguity. The coverage of rook Checkerboard, for which $\tau$ is not identified, rose from 0.150 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.464 at $\tau = 3$, because its intervals widened around the wrong quantity (Appendix \ref{app:technical-notes}). Appendix \ref{app:supp-comparisons} shows coverage across $\tau$ for each design.

## Variation across parameter settings

Table \ref{tab:robustness} gives the distribution of MSE across the 160 queen blocks at $\tau = 1$. Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lowest median (0.080) and the lowest worst-case MSE of any design (0.169). Isolation Buffer had the narrowest range (0.128 to 0.206), because its MSE does not depend on the spillover regime, but at a higher median than the two leading designs. Balanced Quartiles had a low median (0.115) and a worst case of 0.290. The distributions of $2\times2$ Blocking and Checkerboard reflected their dependence on the spillover regime: both had low first quartiles (0.062 and 0.063) and high upper quartiles (0.580 and 2.093). Checkerboard had the highest MSE in all 80 control-only blocks. In the 80 both-arms blocks, the highest MSE belonged to High Incidence Focus in 42 and to Isolation Buffer in 38. Under rook contiguity, Incidence-Guided Saturation also had the lowest worst-case MSE (0.138). These worst cases summarize variation across parameter settings. They are distinct from the conditional risk across assignments within one setting, examined next.

## Allocation-specific risk

The mean is only part of the comparison, because a trial realizes a single allocation. Under control-only spillover, the worst 10\% of SRS allocations on the grid had mean conditional MSE 60\% above that of the average SRS allocation (0.3462 against 0.2165). The saturation designs' worst-decile MSE was 0.54 to 0.55 times SRS's on the grid and 0.64 to 0.68 times in NC. Under both-arms spillover, their worst-decile MSE was 1.06 to 1.07 times SRS's on the grid and 0.93 to 0.94 times in NC (Table \ref{tab:downside}), so the small mean disadvantage there comes with no worse downside in NC.

Averaged over the 200 units per regime (fixed surfaces crossed with the extreme combinations of $\rho$ and $\gamma$), Incidence-Guided Saturation's control-only mean MSE was 0.1402 against 0.2165 for SRS. Its estimated 90th percentile of allocation-specific MSE was 0.1733 against 0.2962, and its estimated worst-decile mean was 0.1912 against 0.3462, lower than SRS in all 200 units on both measures. Under both arms, the corresponding mean MSE was 0.0457 against 0.0427 and the worst-decile mean 0.0583 against 0.0544. Saturation Quadrants also performed favorably under control-only spillover. Table \ref{tab:downside} in the application section compares every design with SRS on both criteria. These results at the extreme parameter settings support a qualified downside argument for saturation. They do not replace the full grid benchmark. The precision check preserved the control-only direction, but outcome noise contributed substantially to the estimated variation across allocations, especially under both arms. Quantiles and worst-decile membership estimated from a finite number of outcomes remain uncertain. We therefore use the completed NC application below as the next setting-specific assessment rather than extrapolate exact tail protection from these settings.

## Rook contiguity

Under rook contiguity at $\tau = 1$, pooled over the five incidence configurations, the mean-MSE order was Incidence-Guided Saturation (0.072), Balanced Quartiles (0.084), $2\times2$ Blocking (0.128), Isolation Buffer (0.133), High Incidence Focus (0.206), and Checkerboard (0.480) (Table \ref{tab:performance}; Figure \ref{fig:mse-rook} in Appendix \ref{app:rook-figures}). The same order held within each of the five incidence configurations (Table \ref{tab:by-config}). Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lowest MSE in 97 of the 160 rook blocks (61\%) and Balanced Quartiles in 60 (38\%). Coverage was between 0.948 and 0.952 for every design except Checkerboard, whose coverage was 0.162 (Figure \ref{fig:coverage-rook} in Appendix \ref{app:rook-figures}). With SRS as a seventh member, the Friedman test rejected equal ranks ($\chi^2 = 795.77$, $\text{df} = 6$, 160 blocks, $p < 2.2\times10^{-16}$). Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon tests separated every pair except two: Balanced Quartiles against SRS, and $2\times2$ Blocking against Isolation Buffer, which were close and traded places at some values of $\tau$. Nemenyi comparisons also left Incidence-Guided Saturation, Balanced Quartiles and SRS unseparated from one another. Incidence-Guided Saturation nevertheless had the lower MSE in 48 of the 50 independent configuration-by-surface units against Balanced Quartiles (Appendix \ref{app:supp-comparisons}), and its paired comparisons with SRS within each regime appear under Comparison with simple random sampling.

Checkerboard under rook contiguity is a different case: $\tau$ is not identified, and the coefficient on $Z$ estimates $\tau - \gamma$ (Methods). At $\tau = 1$, Checkerboard's mean bias was $-0.502$, $-0.600$, $-0.704$, and $-0.802$ at $\gamma = 0.5$, 0.6, 0.7, and 0.8, while its mean standard deviation stayed between 0.20 and 0.21. Squared bias, averaged over scenarios, accounted for 0.438 of its MSE of 0.480 (Figure \ref{fig:biasvar-rook} in Appendix \ref{app:rook-figures}). Its coverage fell from 0.337 at $\gamma = 0.5$ to 0.031 at $\gamma = 0.8$, and was between 0.146 and 0.171 at every level of $\rho$, against 0.949 to 0.952 under queen contiguity (Table \ref{tab:checkerboard-coverage} in Appendix \ref{app:sensitivity-tables}). Because $WZ = 1 - Z$, the two spillover regimes define the same outcome model. The observed MSEs, 0.477 under the both-arms regime and 0.483 under the control-only regime, differ only by Monte Carlo error. Under rook contiguity, Checkerboard's estimates were precise but centered on the wrong quantity. Under queen contiguity, they were imprecise but valid. We keep these estimates in every ranking and flag them.

## Non-oracle sensitivity analysis

The non-oracle model, which omits the spillover term, was biased for every design. Table \ref{tab:oracle-nonoracle} in Appendix \ref{app:oracle-nonoracle} gives both models' MSE, bias, and coverage for each design. At $\tau = 1$, and setting aside Checkerboard under rook contiguity, its bias ranged from $-0.12$ to $-0.40$ and its coverage from 0.54 to 0.91 across designs and neighbor types. For Checkerboard under rook contiguity, the two models coincide: once the aliased spillover column is dropped, the oracle model is the non-oracle model. Omitting the spillover term also removes a column that can be nearly collinear with $Z$, and the non-oracle estimates were accordingly less variable for some designs. Under queen contiguity, the non-oracle MSE was lower than the oracle MSE for every design, most of all for Checkerboard (oracle 1.087, non-oracle 0.108) and $2\times2$ Blocking (oracle 0.319, non-oracle 0.121). Under rook contiguity it was higher for every design except $2\times2$ Blocking (0.128 under both models) and Checkerboard (identical). Where a design's non-oracle MSE was lower, however, its estimate was biased and its intervals under-covered, so the lower MSE does not support valid inference. These results do not change the recommendation: Incidence-Guided Saturation also had the lowest non-oracle MSE under both neighbor types (0.087 under queen contiguity and 0.086 under rook contiguity).

# Application to sudden unexpected death in North Carolina

This section repeats the design comparison on the observed North Carolina geography to inform planning of the SUD-prevention education pilot. It uses the outcome model, designs, estimator and performance criteria of the Methods. The first four subsections describe the observed inputs and the changes this setting requires, and the last four report the results.

## Purpose and observed inputs

The application asks which allocation designs estimate a known education-intervention effect accurately on this geography, when some designs use historical SUD incidence to direct treatment. It supports planning an education intervention for healthcare professionals involved in SUD prevention. The application uses no observed intervention outcomes and no estimated relationship between local SUD incidence and education ability. Any eventual effect on SUD incidence requires a separate clinical evaluation. A real pilot might realize only one allocation per planning year, so both average estimation error and the risk of a poor allocation matter.

The assignment units are 58 community college service-area clusters that partition North Carolina's 100 counties under the study mapping (Figure \ref{fig:service-areas}). Northampton is assigned to Halifax Community College, Bertie to Martin Community College, and Hertford alone to Roanoke-Chowan Community College. These county-to-college assignments are analysis conventions, not exclusive service commitments. Observed county-year deaths at ages 18--64, and population estimates for the same ages from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results program [@seer_population_data], were aggregated to the same named clusters for each year, 2018--2021. SUD deaths were identified from death certificates with the case-adjudication algorithm of Gan and colleagues [@gan_factors_2019]. The corrected numerator supplied by Habib includes heart-failure deaths formerly excluded as presumed non-sudden. It totals 23,523 deaths over 25,594,321 person-years. The earlier numerator reproduces the totals behind Habib's unpublished report [@habib_temporal_2026]. The application uses the corrected numerator. We do not infer undocumented upstream exclusion rules or zip-code allocation from the received county panel.

Annual incidence is $100,000D_{iy}/P_{iy}$, and pooled incidence is $100,000\sum_yD_{iy}/\sum_yP_{iy}$, with the latter population sum interpreted as person-years. All 58 clusters are present in each year, and counts and populations sum back to statewide totals. We hold these observed annual surfaces fixed, generate no synthetic incidence surface and report years separately (Figure \ref{fig:nc-observed}). The county death-certificate source data are restricted and not publicly available. We report only 58-cluster summaries. The data were obtained under University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill Institutional Review Board protocol 14-2036, "Sudden Unexpected Death in North Carolina" (principal investigator Ross J. Simpson, Jr., Department of Medicine).

## Geographic adaptations and treatment budgets

Queen contiguity between service areas, computed from legal county boundaries, defines primary adjacency, and rook contiguity is a sensitivity analysis. Shared legal boundaries across water can create adjacency. Adjacency here is a prespecified geographic proxy for exposure, not a measured network of professional communication.

All eight designs and SRS are evaluated under the names used on the grid, adapted to the irregular map. Appendix \ref{app:nc} gives the rules in full and maps the fixed regions and example assignments. Checkerboard becomes a deterministic greedy graph-coloring assignment, an interspersion analog rather than a literal rectangular checkerboard or an exact bipartite coloring. High Incidence Focus treats the 29 highest annual-rate clusters, Isolation Buffer draws a greedy random maximal independent set on the NC adjacency graph, SRS treats a random 29 of 58 clusters, and Balanced Quartiles and Balanced Halves stratify annual rate ranks and treat 29 overall. The two saturation designs use one fixed four-region partition for all years, chosen for geographic compactness and balance without consulting outcomes. Saturation Quadrants randomly assigns 20/40/60/80\% to these regions in each draw. Incidence-Guided Saturation ranks the regions by the mean rank of their clusters' annual per-capita rates and assigns 80/60/40/20\% from highest to lowest. Mean raw rates and pooled regional rates serve as prespecified alternative regional summaries. On the NC map, $2\times2$ Blocking uses spatial blocks of nearby clusters, 14 irregular groups formed once per year, and treats half of each group, rounded, at random. Treatment budgets, the numbers of treated clusters, therefore differ across designs. We report them (Table \ref{tab:nc-budgets}) rather than modify the designs to force equal budgets.

## Outcome model, evaluation and sensitivity analyses

For the primary education outcome, we set $\beta=0$ in Equation \ref{eq:outcome}, use the 58-cluster $W$, and fix $\tau=1$, $\sigma=1$:
\begin{equation}
Y=(I-\rho W)^{-1}[\tau Z+S(Z)+\epsilon],\qquad \epsilon\sim N(0,I).
\label{eq:nc-education}
\end{equation}
Observed incidence affects assignments but neither baseline education nor the constant structural intervention effect. We estimate $\tau$ with the same validated maximum likelihood implementation as in the grid study, with an intercept, $Z$ and the true regime-specific $S(Z)$, without $X$. As in the grid model, $\tau$ is the coefficient before spatial propagation, not an average total effect after applying $(I-\rho W)^{-1}$. For the main application and for the analyses of partial participation and sample size below, we report $\hat\tau \pm t_{0.975,\,n-p}\,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}\sqrt{n/(n-p)}$, where $n$ is the number of participating colleges and $p$ the number of fitted coefficients plus $\rho$. We test $\tau = 0$ against the same $t$ distribution. The maximum likelihood variance divides by $n$, and the normal reference distribution ignores the estimated parameters. With 58 or fewer clusters, both make the Wald interval too narrow.

Primary queen settings cross $\rho=0,0.2,0.5$, $\gamma=0.5,0.8$, both regimes, four years and nine designs (432 reported settings). A matched hypothetical baseline sensitivity adds $X=(\operatorname{rank}_{\rm average}(rate)-0.5)/58$ with $\beta=1$ to both the outcome baseline and the fitted covariates (432 settings). It changes baseline and adjustment together and is not an empirical incidence--education association. A rook-contiguity sensitivity analysis of the primary model uses the extreme values $\rho=0,0.5$ (288 settings), and the two alternative regional summaries add 96 Incidence-Guided Saturation settings. The full application reports 1,248 settings, computed from 936 distinct simulation settings, because reported settings with the same allocations and outcome model share one simulation.

We sampled $J=100$ assignments and simulated $R=100$ independent outcomes per distinct assignment. A design with only one possible assignment instead received $R=1,000$ outcomes for that assignment, rather than 100 repeated copies of it counted as separate allocations. A prespecified adaptive schedule extended allocations or outcomes where needed until the Monte Carlo standard error of mean MSE was at most 5\% of mean MSE and that of coverage at most 0.01. Two single-assignment settings in the matched sensitivity analysis required $R=2,000$, and all randomized designs met these targets at $J=100$ and $R=100$ (Appendix \ref{app:nc}). In the primary model, Checkerboard, Saturation Quadrants, Isolation Buffer and SRS reuse the same simulations across years, because annual incidence enters neither their allocation nor the outcome model. These repeated values are not independent annual confirmation.

For each allocation $a$, the repeated outcomes estimate the conditional MSE $m(a)=E_\epsilon[(\hat\tau-\tau)^2\mid a,\text{observed inputs}]$, the expected squared error of the estimate if $a$ were the allocation realized. We report its distribution across sampled allocations, its estimated 90th percentile and the estimated mean among the worst 10\% of sampled allocations, alongside unconditional mean MSE, bias and coverage. A separate tail refinement at queen $\rho=0,0.5$, $\gamma=0.8$, both regimes and all years and designs kept the same allocations and extended the randomized designs to $R=400$ outcomes per allocation, keeping $R=1,000$ for single-assignment designs. Worst-decile assignments were identified with one half of the simulated outcomes and evaluated with the other half, to avoid selection bias. We recorded design-matrix rank, residual treatment information, aliased columns, warnings, invalid estimates or intervals, and boundary estimates of $\rho$.

We compared the nine strategies with the Friedman, Nemenyi and Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon tests used on the grid, treating the 24 combinations of year, $\rho$ and $\gamma$ as blocks, separately for each spillover regime and each value of $\beta$. The four years share one map and the strategies whose allocations ignore annual incidence share their simulations across years, so these $p$-values summarize consistency rather than independent evidence.

To check that the design comparison does not depend on the spatial model, we generated data at $N = 58$ with $\beta = 0$ from the spatial lag model and fitted them with both a conditional autoregressive (CAR) model [@besag_spatial_1974; @cressie_statistics_1993] and the spatial lag model. In the reverse direction, we generated data from a CAR model with the same mean and fitted them with both models. We also fitted two Bayesian models to the spatial lag data, a CAR model with the prior of Leroux and colleagues [@leroux_estimation_2000; @lee_carbayes_2013] and a Bayesian spatial lag model [@lesage_introduction_2009]. Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext} gives the four models, their priors, the Markov chain Monte Carlo settings and the convergence checks. Finally, we replaced the proportional spillover exposure by a binary indicator of any treated neighbor and by a count of treated neighbors scaled by the mean number of neighbors, with the same form in the outcome model and the fit.

## Partial participation and sample size

All 58 colleges will be invited to take part after the pilot, but not every college will join. We therefore repeated the application for subsets of $N$ participating colleges, $N \in \{15, 20, 25, 29, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 58\}$, under the education outcome model with $\beta = 0$. Under random volunteering, 50 subsets were drawn for each $N$ and shared by every design and year, so designs are compared on the same participants. In a sensitivity analysis at $N = 20$ and $N = 29$, a college's chance of joining rose linearly with its incidence rank, so that the highest-burden college was three times as likely to join as the lowest. Each design was rebuilt on the participants with its own rule, and the four saturation regions were required to contain at least two colleges each. Spatial dependence links participating colleges only, so a participant with no participating neighbor has a zero row in the participants' weights matrix $W_P$. Spillover exposure counts treated participating neighbors over all geographic neighbors, $e_j(Z) = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{N}(j)} Z_k / |\mathcal{N}(j)|$, so a non-participating neighbor counts as untreated. Spillover scales with the effect, $\gamma = \kappa\tau$ with $\kappa \in \{0.5, 0.8\}$, and the effect $\tau$ took nine values from 0 to 2 in units of the college-level outcome standard deviation. Settings crossed these with $\rho \in \{0, 0.5\}$, both spillover regimes, the nine strategies and the four planning years. With fewer than 58 participants, each setting used 20 allocations and 10 outcomes on each of the 50 subsets (10,000 fits), and a design with a single possible allocation on a subset used 200 outcomes instead. With all 58 colleges, each setting used 100 allocations and 100 outcomes, as in the main application, and reproduced that application's MSE and coverage within Monte Carlo error. All effect sizes share the same subsets, allocations and noise, so power curves are smooth in $\tau$. For each setting we estimated three quantities with the corrected $t$ test above: power, the number of colleges needed for 80\% power, and the smallest effect detectable with 80\% power at each $N$.

The trial outcome is a score measured on each trained professional and averaged within each college. We write a professional's score as a college effect plus individual variation, with total variance 1, so that effects are in individual standard-deviation units. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) is the share of that variance that lies between colleges, so the between-college variance is the ICC and the within-college variance is $1 - \text{ICC}$. Averaging the scores of $m$ professionals leaves the college part unchanged and divides the individual part by $m$, so the college mean has standard deviation $\sigma_c = \sqrt{\text{ICC} + (1 - \text{ICC})/m}$ [@donner_design_2000; @hayes_cluster_2017]. A college-level effect of $\tau$ standard deviations is therefore an individual-level standardized effect $d = \tau\sigma_c$. With $\beta = 0$, multiplying the effect and the noise by the same constant leaves $\hat\tau/\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}$ unchanged, so power for any $m$, ICC and $d$ follows from the simulated college-level results. Rerunning one setting with the effect and the noise both halved reproduced its estimates to within $6\times10^{-8}$. In a sensitivity analysis, the number of trained professionals grew with college population ($m$ averaging 25 over participants, ICC $= 0.05$), so the noise variance differed between colleges. The fitted model stayed unweighted, as an analyst unaware of the difference would fit it.

## Accuracy, coverage and reach

The main run generated 7,598,000 independent outcome fits. Every setting is complete and meets its prespecified precision targets for mean MSE and coverage: the largest relative Monte Carlo standard error of mean MSE is 0.04871 and the largest Monte Carlo standard error of coverage is 0.00892. No setting produced warnings, aliased columns, estimates of $\rho$ at the boundary of its parameter space or estimation failures. The tail refinement adds 2,280,000 independent outcomes. Counting the outcomes reused from the main run only once gives 9,878,000 distinct outcomes across the two stages. Monte Carlo precision describes uncertainty in simulated performance, not interval calibration.

Figure \ref{fig:nc-mse} compares the eight designs with SRS by year and regime. Under control-only spillover, Saturation Quadrants has descriptive mean MSE 0.22329 against SRS 0.30761, a 27.4\% reduction. Incidence-Guided Saturation reduces mean MSE by 21.1--29.9\% across the four observed years (Table \ref{tab:nc-year}). Both saturation designs have lower mean MSE than SRS in every primary parameter setting, and approximate Monte Carlo intervals for each setting-specific difference excluded zero. Neither is uniquely best: as on the grid, the two performed similarly, and their advantage over SRS comes from the saturation structure both designs share. Under control-only spillover, the performance of High Incidence Focus depends on the year, so we cannot recommend it for every year.

Under both-arms spillover, SRS mean MSE is 0.07638, Saturation Quadrants 0.07518, and Incidence-Guided Saturation ranges from 0.07428 to 0.07682 across years. SRS remains competitive with balancing, blocking and saturation. Small point differences do not establish equivalence or universal optimality. High Incidence Focus has low both-arms MSE in the primary model, but its allocation is deterministic for these fixed rates. Its low MSE is model-based accuracy conditional on that allocation, not evidence of randomization-based causal validity.

Mean coverage of the 95\% intervals across the four years was between 94.1\% and 94.9\% for every design and regime, and between 94.1\% and 95.1\% in single years. The Wald interval covered only 92.6\% to 93.6\% (Table \ref{tab:interval-comparison}). Meeting the Monte Carlo precision targets did not repair that finite-sample undercoverage, but the corrected $t$ interval described under Outcome model, evaluation and sensitivity analyses did (Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext}). Appendix \ref{app:nc} gives bias and coverage for every year, design and regime. Checkerboard's treatment effect is identified on this irregular graph, but weak treatment--spillover separation makes its estimates imprecise. On the rectangular grid under rook contiguity, by contrast, $\tau$ is not identified for Checkerboard.

Population shares put these results in context (Table \ref{tab:nc-budgets}). High Incidence Focus treats 29 clusters but only about 22--24\% of working-age population, while Isolation Buffer treats a mean of 15.89 clusters and about 27\%. These population denominators measure geographic reach, not the number of healthcare professionals educated, intervention cost or participant-level precision.

Incidence-Guided Saturation sends more treatment to high-incidence regions when incidence differs between regions. On the NC map it differs little, because the four regions' mean incidence ranks lie between 24 and 34 of 58 in every year. On average, Incidence-Guided Saturation treats colleges holding 51.1\% of the summed college incidence rates, against 50.4\% for Saturation Quadrants and 62.2\% for High Incidence Focus. Shares of deaths run the other way (49.2\%, 49.6\% and 35.4\%), because the highest-rate colleges serve small populations. On the simulation grid, where regional incidence differed more, incidence guidance raised the treated share of incidence by 2.1 to 3.1 percentage points over Saturation Quadrants, and across surfaces the gain rose with the spread of the regions' mean incidence ranks (correlation 0.84 to 0.99; Figure \ref{fig:spread-gain} in Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext}).

## Allocation-specific risk in North Carolina

At the two refined queen settings, $\rho=0$ and $\rho=0.5$ with $\gamma=0.8$, under control-only spillover, Saturation Quadrants' estimated 90th percentile of allocation-specific MSE is 31.8--32.9\% below SRS and its estimated worst-decile mean 34.6--37.8\% below. Incidence-Guided Saturation's corresponding reductions are 20.8--38.6\% and 20.7--43.4\%. The pattern persists under the split-half evaluation described above. Figure \ref{fig:nc-risk} in Appendix \ref{app:nc} shows the $\rho=0.5$ setting. These reductions support a descriptive downside benefit alongside lower average error, conditional on the studied model and sampled assignments.

Table \ref{tab:downside} compares every design with SRS on both criteria, mean conditional MSE and the mean of the worst 10\% of sampled allocations, on the grid and at the refined NC settings. Under control-only spillover, both saturation designs had lower mean and worst-decile MSE than SRS in both settings. Isolation Buffer also had a lower worst decile than SRS under control-only spillover (0.62 of SRS on the grid and 0.91 in NC). Under both-arms spillover, its mean was 3.80 and 3.69 times that of SRS, and it treated fewer clusters. High Incidence Focus has a single allocation in NC. That allocation's MSE was below the SRS worst-decile mean under both regimes (0.76 under both arms and 0.64 under control-only spillover), with mean MSE close to SRS (0.93 and 1.03). On the grid, however, its both-arms mean was 3.81 times that of SRS, and its NC result depends on the incidence model, as the matched sensitivity analysis below shows. Balanced Quartiles and Balanced Halves matched SRS on both criteria. Checkerboard and $2\times2$ Blocking did not improve on SRS on either criterion in any setting.

```

Figure \ref{fig:alloc-dist} shows the full allocation-to-allocation distribution for the six designs and SRS. Under control-only spillover, most Incidence-Guided Saturation allocations had lower MSE than the average SRS allocation in both studies, whereas the SRS distribution extended well above its mean.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[!htb]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/compact/allocation_distribution_by_design.pdf}

Simulation study: grid allocation-risk study at $\tau=1$, 200 fixed surface/parameter settings per spillover regime. Application study: refined NC settings ($\rho=0, 0.5$; $\gamma=0.8$) in each year 2018--2021. For each allocation, MSE is estimated from repeated simulated outcomes (100 in the simulation study, at least 400 in the application study). Thin lines span the 5th to 95th percentiles of allocations and thick bars the 25th to 75th; circles mark the mean. The tail estimates remain uncertain. With $J=100$, the worst decile contains only ten sampled draws. Extra outcomes reduce noise in $\hat m(a)$ but do not enlarge the allocation sample. All 112 reported settings in the tail refinement for designs with more than one possible assignment flag uncertain worst-decile membership. Under both arms, the Jaccard index of the worst deciles identified by the two outcome halves (allocations in both divided by allocations in either) was 0--0.25 for Incidence-Guided Saturation, and approximately 61--86\% of the raw variance of estimated risk across allocations was attributable to outcome Monte Carlo noise. Saturation Quadrants' worst-decile membership was similarly unstable. Small both-arms tail differences therefore do not establish superior downside protection. Checkerboard and High Incidence Focus each have only one possible assignment for these inputs. Their 90th percentile and worst-decile mean equal their conditional mean MSE, which does not imply low error or absence of outcome uncertainty.


## Sensitivity analyses

In the matched hypothetical sensitivity analysis, which adds incidence to the baseline and adjusts for it, High Incidence Focus MSE rises to roughly 3.68--4.44 times its primary value under both arms and 1.42--2.52 times under control-only spillover. Because this design treats the highest-incidence clusters, adjusting for incidence leaves less residual treatment information. This sensitivity analysis changes baseline and adjustment jointly and does not imply that SUD incidence predicts education ability. Rook and queen comparisons matched at the same extreme combinations of $\rho$ and $\gamma$ preserve broad regime-specific conclusions. Alternative regional summaries change the regional ordering in some years. Where an alternative summary gives the same ordering and ties, it gives the same set of possible assignments and so the same results. We retain the prespecified mean-rank rule rather than select a summary retrospectively. Appendix \ref{app:nc} reports the matched sensitivity table and regional ordering.

The design comparison did not depend on the spatial model used to generate or fit the data, with one exception (Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext}). Fitting a CAR model, generating the data from a CAR model, or both, left the saturation designs with 0.76 to 0.82 times SRS's MSE under control-only spillover. Checkerboard and Isolation Buffer were still the worst designs under both-arms spillover. A Bayesian spatial lag model reproduced the maximum likelihood results, with posterior means correlated 0.999 with the maximum likelihood estimates, credible-interval coverage of 94.6\% to 95.3\% and the same design ordering. The exception is the Bayesian CAR model with strong spatial dependence ($\rho = 0.5$). Its estimates were biased by 0.14 to 0.22 even when its chains converged, its coverage was 88\% to 90\%, and it did not reproduce the saturation designs' control-only advantage. That model assumes a different dependence structure from the one that generated the data, and the correctly specified Bayesian model does not share the problem. Under a binary spillover exposure Isolation Buffer was never identified, and under a count exposure the saturation designs remained the best under control-only spillover. Formal tests over the 24 combinations of year, $\rho$ and $\gamma$ rejected equal ranks for every regime and value of $\beta$ (Friedman $\chi^2$ from 135 to 180 on 8 degrees of freedom), and under control-only spillover the two saturation designs had the two best average ranks.

## Colleges needed under partial participation

Under both-arms spillover, the design hardly affected the number of colleges a trial needs. Every design except Checkerboard and Isolation Buffer needed 35 to 37 colleges for 80\% power to detect a college-level effect of one standard deviation, and about 19 colleges for 1.5 standard deviations (Figure \ref{fig:colleges-needed}, Table \ref{tab:nc-power}). Checkerboard and Isolation Buffer did not reach 80\% power at $\tau = 1$ even with all 58 colleges. Under control-only spillover, no design reached 80\% power at $\tau = 1$ with all 58 colleges. At $\tau = 1.5$ the two saturation designs needed 28 colleges, against 29 to 32 for SRS and the rank-based designs (High Incidence Focus, Balanced Quartiles and Balanced Halves). At that effect, $2\times2$ Blocking and Isolation Buffer failed to reach 80\% power with 58 colleges in one of the four planning years. Power under control-only spillover rose slowly beyond about 40 colleges (Figure \ref{fig:power-n}). When nearly every college participates, nearly every control has a treated neighbor, so spillover exposure varies little and is hard to separate from treatment. Non-participating neighbors restore some of that variation, and so do the saturation designs. With all 58 colleges, the smallest effect detectable with 80\% power under both-arms spillover was 0.76 to 0.78 college-level standard deviations for every design except Checkerboard (1.32) and Isolation Buffer (1.50). Under control-only spillover it was 1.24 to 1.25 for the two saturation designs, against 1.45 to 1.57 for SRS and the rank-based designs.

Random volunteering, $\rho = 0.5$ and spillover $\gamma = 0.8\tau$. Dark bars show the mean over the 2018--2021 planning years and whiskers the range. Light bars mark designs that did not reach 80\% power with all 58 colleges in the stated number of years, with the smallest number needed in the other years.}
