With $m = 25$ trained professionals per college and an ICC of 0.05, $\sigma_c = 0.30$. Under both-arms spillover, an individual-level effect of $d = 0.3$ then gives power 0.71 to 0.72 with 29 colleges and 0.96 with 58, for SRS and for both saturation designs. Under control-only spillover the same effect gives power 0.49 and 0.53 with SRS, and 0.51 and 0.64 with Incidence-Guided Saturation (Table \ref{tab:nc-translation} in Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext}). Letting the number of professionals grow with college population, at the same average of 25, reduced power by about 0.1 for every design and changed no design's relative standing.

The Wald test rejected a true null hypothesis in 11\% to 13\% of simulated trials with 15 colleges and in 6\% to 7\% with 58. With the corrected $t$ test the rejection rate was 4.4\% to 5.6\%. The coverage of the corrected interval at $\tau = 1$ was between 94.0\% and 95.6\% for every design and regime at every number of colleges (Table \ref{tab:nc-calibration} in Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext}). The colleges-needed numbers above therefore come from a test with the nominal size.

The regime-specific guidance held with fewer participants, but the size of the saturation advantage depended on participation (Table \ref{tab:nc-guidance} in Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext}). Checkerboard and Isolation Buffer remained worse than SRS under both-arms spillover at every number of colleges, and the rank-based designs' mean MSE was within 2\% of that of SRS, except High Incidence Focus with 40 and 58 colleges (4\% and 8\% below). Under control-only spillover, the saturation designs' mean MSE was 22\% below that of SRS with 58 colleges, 9\% to 10\% below with 40, 4\% to 5\% below with 29 and about 1\% below with 20. With few participants, non-participating neighbors already create the exposure variation that saturation otherwise supplies. When the colleges with higher incidence were more likely to volunteer, the saturation designs' advantage over SRS was 2\% or less at 20 and 29 colleges. Isolation Buffer went from matching SRS under control-only spillover with 58 colleges to 2.3 times SRS's MSE with 29 colleges and 6.2 times with 15.

The application supports considering either saturation strategy when control-only spillover is plausible, and SRS alongside other randomized strategies when both-arm exposure is expected. A trial team should consider likely spillover, recruitment, cluster and participant budgets, achievable measurement precision and interval calibration before selecting one realized allocation. The findings do not establish intervention effectiveness or a final trial protocol.

# Discussion

## Summary of findings

We compared six treatment assignment designs in the detailed grid ranking, plus two related variants and SRS, for a spatial cluster randomized trial on a grid of 100 clusters. The comparison covered three mechanisms of heterogeneous baseline incidence, two spillover regimes, and a range of values for spatial dependence, spillover magnitude, and the treatment effect. Some findings held across the incidence configurations and the values of $\rho$, $\gamma$, and $\tau$ under queen contiguity. Others depended on the spillover regime, which a trial team may not know in advance.

We judged each design on two criteria: its average MSE, and the spread of MSE across the allocations it can produce. A trial realizes one allocation, so a design with a low average MSE can still give a poor estimate if some of its allocations perform badly. Chapter 2 compared simple random and block stratified sampling on the same two criteria. The spread matters most for SRS under control-only spillover: on the grid, the worst 10\% of SRS allocations had mean conditional MSE 0.3462, against 0.2165 for SRS allocations overall.

Under queen contiguity, Incidence-Guided Saturation had the lowest mean squared error (0.091) and Balanced Quartiles the second lowest (0.131), and the same two designs led under rook contiguity (0.072 and 0.084). Under queen contiguity, the order of the six designs was the same in each of the five incidence configurations and at every value of $\tau$, and neither the strength of spatial dependence in the outcome nor the spillover magnitude changed it. The mechanism that generated the incidence surface changed each design's MSE by under 10\%, except for High Incidence Focus. Coverage of the 95\% intervals was close to 0.95 for every design under both neighbor types, except Checkerboard under rook contiguity, so the designs differed in precision and coverage did not separate them.

The spillover regime was the one factor that changed the queen ranking. Under queen contiguity at $\tau = 1$, Checkerboard and $2\times2$ Blocking were close to the best designs when spillover reached both arms and were the two worst when it reached only control clusters (MSE 0.062 and 2.111 for Checkerboard, 0.062 and 0.576 for $2\times2$ Blocking). Balanced Quartiles also lost ground under the control-only regime (0.042 and 0.219). Incidence-Guided Saturation, by contrast, was first or second among the six detailed designs under both regimes at every value of $\tau$, with a both-arms MSE 8\% above that of SRS. Its control-only MSE did rise with $\tau$, and Isolation Buffer, whose MSE did not, matched or passed it under that regime at $\tau = 2$ and passed it at $\tau = 3$. For a design whose performance depends on the regime, average MSE does not show the risk of choosing it when the regime is unknown.

Checkerboard, the strict allocation of Chapter 2, failed for different reasons under the two neighbor types. Under queen contiguity its estimates stayed centered on $\tau$ with close to nominal coverage but were imprecise, because under the control-only regime only the boundary clusters separate the spillover effect from the treatment effect. Under rook contiguity, $\tau$ is not identified, and its estimates were centered on $\tau - \gamma$. Checkerboard intersperses treated and control clusters as finely as the grid allows, and both failures come from the dependence this pattern creates between $Z$ and the spillover covariate (Methods).

These are design-stage results, and they complement analysis-stage modeling rather than replace it. Every design was analyzed with a spatial lag model that included the spillover term. In the grid study, the estimates were close to unbiased for every design whose $\tau$ was identified: at $\tau = 1$, the absolute bias of each design under each regime was at most 0.048 under queen contiguity and 0.027 under rook contiguity. Given that model, the choice of design determined how precisely $\tau$ was estimated.

## Design guidance by spillover regime

Together, the grid benchmark, the allocation-risk results (Table \ref{tab:downside}) and the NC application give guidance by scenario. When spillover is expected to reach mainly control clusters, Incidence-Guided Saturation and Saturation Quadrants had the lowest mean MSE and among the lowest worst-decile MSE, so they are the designs we recommend over SRS. Isolation Buffer also limited downside in that regime, but it should be considered only when both-arms spillover is implausible and a smaller treated budget is acceptable. When spillover is expected to reach both arms, the spread of MSE across allocations was small for SRS and the balancing and saturation designs. SRS, Balanced Quartiles and Balanced Halves performed about equally. The saturation designs had mean MSE 4\% to 8\% above SRS on the grid and within 3\% of it in NC, with worst-decile MSE within 7\% of SRS's in both, so SRS and the saturation designs are both reasonable choices. The number of colleges a trial needs depends far more on the spillover regime than on the design: 35 to 37 colleges detect a one-standard-deviation college-level effect under both-arms spillover with any design except Checkerboard and Isolation Buffer, whereas under control-only spillover even all 58 colleges do not. The saturation designs' advantage over SRS also shrinks as fewer colleges join. High Incidence Focus gave one fixed allocation whose MSE in NC was below the SRS worst-decile mean under both regimes. Its accuracy is model-based rather than randomization-based, however. On the grid, its both-arms MSE was about four times that of SRS. Its MSE also rose 1.4--4.4-fold when baseline outcomes were related to incidence. It is a candidate only when historical incidence can be assumed unrelated to the outcome. Checkerboard and $2\times2$ Blocking did not improve on SRS on either criterion. The NC model assesses education outcomes rather than assuming that historical SUD incidence predicts education ability or a heterogeneous intervention effect.

Saturation Quadrants, which assigns the same saturations without reference to incidence, performed similarly to Incidence-Guided Saturation (see Treatment assignment designs). Their accuracy advantage over SRS under control-only spillover therefore comes from the shared saturation structure, and incidence guidance lets a trial direct its highest treatment saturations to the highest-incidence regions with little or no loss of estimation accuracy. How much treatment it redirects depends on how much incidence differs between regions, a few percentage points of incidence share on the grid and less than one on the NC map, whose regions have similar incidence.

## Relation to Chapter 2

Chapter 2's practical argument considered reasonably good estimation together with protection against poor allocation in the small-grid settings it studied. We preserve both criteria while extending the designs, geography and incidence conditions. Our findings concern these new models and settings and do not compare numerical results across chapters directly. The rectangular Checkerboard and its graph adaptation illustrate why a restricted allocation's low assignment variation must be interpreted together with its level of estimation error. The application also separates incidence-guided assignment from assumptions about education outcomes. No direct cross-chapter result comparison is needed to motivate these extensions.

## Limitations

These conclusions have several limitations. First, the primary estimator is an oracle. It includes the exact spillover exposure term, so its results are a best case for each design. We fit a non-oracle model that omits the spillover term as a sensitivity analysis. It was biased for every design and its intervals under-covered, but Incidence-Guided Saturation still had the lowest MSE under both neighbor types. The non-oracle model is only one departure from the oracle. We did not study an analyst who includes a spillover term of the wrong form, such as one built on the wrong neighbor definition or a distance decay.

Second, in the synthetic grid study, the designs and the fitted model used the incidence surface that generated the outcome (the matched-surface assumption in Methods). In practice, planning incidence is estimated from an earlier period and measured with error. The designs that assign treatment by incidence rank, and the covariate adjustment, would then use a noisy surface, and we did not study how that changes the comparison.

Third, in the Poisson mechanism every cluster had the same population of 100,000. Real clusters, including the community college service areas in the Application, differ in population, so their observed rates differ in precision, and unequal populations may change how the designs that use incidence perform. In the application, letting the number of trained professionals grow with college population reduced power by about 0.1 for every design and changed no design's relative standing.

Fourth, the full synthetic comparison uses one regular $10\times10$ grid, with $\beta$ and $\sigma$ fixed at 1. The application adds one irregular 58-cluster geography and unequal observed populations, but is not a systematic sweep over graph sizes, structures or participant budgets. Some grid results depend on its boundary geometry, and the design adaptations in the application also change which assignments are possible.

Fifth, the simulation shares random draws by design. Blocks within an incidence configuration share its ten incidence surfaces, so the block-level tests treat dependent blocks as independent, which is why we also compared adjacent designs over the 50 independent configuration-by-surface units. The five values of $\tau$ also share their draws, so the stability of the design order across $\tau$ is not an independent replication at each value (see Stability across treatment effect sizes). Settings and years that share the same simulations cannot be treated as independent confirmation.

Sixth, the simulation's base rate of 35 per 100,000 is not the rate of the county data described in the Application (see Heterogeneous baseline incidence). We kept it deliberately, because the simulation is a general design study rather than a calibration to one data set. In the Poisson mechanism, incidence enters the designs and the fitted model only through the ranks of the observed rates, so the base rate affects the simulation only through the spatial pattern of those ranks and the number of tied rates.

Seventh, application results are conditional on a continuous education-outcome model with known spillover form and constant structural effect, not an observed education intervention or demonstrated reduction in SUD. Working-age population is a geographic denominator rather than a sample of healthcare professionals. Historical rates are held fixed, so uncertainty in their measurement and changes between planning and implementation are not propagated. The matched baseline sensitivity is hypothetical.

Eighth, the 95\% Wald intervals under-covered in both the grid and the application, and the Wald test was anti-conservative with few colleges. A small-sample correction, a $t$ reference distribution with a degrees-of-freedom-corrected standard error, restored coverage to between 94\% and 96\% for every design in the application at every number of participating colleges (Appendix \ref{app:nc-ext}) and to between 0.946 and 0.952 for every identified design on the grid. We therefore report it in both studies. The finite-outcome allocation-tail estimates do not remove noise from individual risks or establish population worst cases. Budgets also differ, so these are evaluations of the retained strategies, not an equal-cost optimization.

Ninth, the participation analysis assumes that colleges volunteer at random or with probability rising with incidence, and that non-participating colleges neither transmit nor receive spillover.

## Future work

The next trial-design steps are to specify the education endpoint, eligible professionals, implementation budget and plausible spillover network, then assess interval calibration for that protocol before randomization. Additional methodological work could study noisy planning incidence, effect heterogeneity, exposure networks beyond contiguity and a broader set of graph geometries. The trial endpoint here is a measured education score, an intermediate outcome. Designing for a later reduction in SUD incidence would need a count outcome model and is left for future work. A larger allocation sample could make the downside estimates more precise if that precision is needed for a final choice. These would extend the completed application and are not needed to characterize the prespecified settings reported here.

**Random-number streams.** Every random draw in the simulation has its own seed, computed by hashing a key that names the draw. The key lists the draw's type (incidence surface, assignments, or noise) and the parameters that identify it, with numeric values written to a fixed number of decimal places so that equal values always give the same key. The random-number generator and its methods for normal and discrete draws are also fixed explicitly, so the streams do not depend on software defaults. Table \ref{tab:seed-keys} lists the three kinds of draw, the parameters in their keys, and the scenarios that therefore share them. Methods describes the two consequences of this scheme: independence from the order of execution, and common random numbers.

```{=latex}
\midrule
Incidence surface $X_k$ & Incidence mechanism, $\rho_X$, $k$ & Every block, design, and value of $\tau$ of the configuration \\
The $J = 25$ assignments of design $d$ on surface $k$ & Incidence mechanism, $\rho_X$, neighbor type, $\rho$, $\gamma$, spillover regime, $k$, $d$ & All five values of $\tau$ and both estimators \\
The 250 noise vectors of a block & Incidence mechanism, $\rho_X$, neighbor type, $\rho$, $\gamma$, spillover regime & All eight designs, all five values of $\tau$, and both estimators \\

\bottomrule

\end{tabular}

\end{table}
```

**Monte Carlo structure and checkpoints.** Within a scenario, fit $(k, j)$, with $k = 1, \dots, 10$ and $j = 1, \dots, 25$, uses surface $X_k$, assignment $Z_{kj}$, and noise vector $\epsilon_{kj}$, the $(k, j)$ column of the block's $100 \times 250$ noise matrix (see Simulation design, resampling, and metrics). The unit of computation is a combination of incidence configuration, neighbor type, and $\rho$: 40 units, each covering 4 values of $\gamma$, 2 spillover regimes, 8 designs, 5 values of $\tau$, 250 fits, and 2 estimators. The units ran in parallel, and the run was set to stop if any unit failed. Each unit's results are saved together with a record of the parameter settings, the simulation code, and the software versions that produced them. Saved results are reused only if all of these match the current run, so results from different code or settings are never combined.

**Scenario metrics.** For one scenario and estimator, let $f = 1, \dots, n$ index the valid fits, those with a finite estimate and standard error (here every fit was valid, so $n = 250$). Let $L_f, U_f = \hat\tau_f \mp t_{0.975,\,N-p}\,\widehat{\text{SE}}_f\sqrt{N/(N-p)}$, with $N = 100$ clusters and $p$ as defined in Methods (the Wald limits replace the multiplier by $z_{0.975} = \Phi^{-1}(0.975) \approx 1.96$), and let $\bar{\hat\tau} = n^{-1}\sum_f \hat\tau_f$. Then
$$
\text{Bias} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{f=1}^{n}(\hat\tau_f - \tau), \qquad
\text{SD} = \left\{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{f=1}^{n}\left(\hat\tau_f - \bar{\hat\tau}\right)^2\right\}^{1/2}, \qquad
\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{f=1}^{n}(\hat\tau_f - \tau)^2,
$$
$$
\text{Coverage} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{f=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{L_f \le \tau \le U_f\}, \qquad
\text{Power} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{f=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{L_f > 0\},
$$
so that $\text{MSE} = \text{Bias}^2 + (n-1)\,\text{SD}^2/n$.

**Surface-level standard errors.** For $m \in \{\text{Bias}, \text{MSE}, \text{Coverage}, \text{Power}\}$, let $m_k$ be the same formula applied to the valid fits from surface $k$ (here all 25). With $K = 10$ and $s(a_1, \dots, a_K) = \{(K-1)^{-1}\sum_k (a_k - \bar a)^2\}^{1/2}$ the sample standard deviation,
$$
\text{SE}(m) = \frac{s(m_1, \dots, m_K)}{\sqrt{K}}, \qquad m \pm t_{0.975,\,K-1}\,\text{SE}(m).
$$
Because every fit was valid, each surface contributes 25 fits and $m = K^{-1}\sum_k m_k$. For two designs $d$ and $d'$ in the same block at the same $\tau$, the difference is paired at the surface level: with $\Delta_k = m_{d,k} - m_{d',k}$,
$$
\text{SE}(m_d - m_{d'}) = \frac{s(\Delta_1, \dots, \Delta_K)}{\sqrt{K}},
$$
with the same $t_{0.975,\,K-1}$ interval.

**Standard errors pooled over configurations.** For one design, neighbor type, and value of $\tau$, let $\mathcal{B}_c$ be the 32 blocks of configuration $c$ and $m_{b,k}$ the surface-$k$ metric in block $b$. The configuration-by-surface means and the pooled metric are
$$
\bar m_{c,k} = \frac{1}{32}\sum_{b \in \mathcal{B}_c} m_{b,k}, \qquad
\bar m = \frac{1}{50}\sum_{c=1}^{5}\sum_{k=1}^{10}\bar m_{c,k},
$$
where $\bar m$ equals the mean of the metric over the 160 scenarios, and
$$
\text{SE}(\bar m) = \frac{s(\{\bar m_{c,k}\})}{\sqrt{50}},
$$
with $s$ taken over the 50 values $\bar m_{c,k}$. These are the standard errors in Table \ref{tab:performance}. For two designs $d$ and $d'$ adjacent in the mean-MSE order (Design performance under queen contiguity), let $D_{c,k} = \bar m_{d,c,k} - \bar m_{d',c,k}$ for $m = \text{MSE}$. The interval for the mean difference is $\bar D \pm t_{0.975,\,49}\, s(\{D_{c,k}\})/\sqrt{50}$, and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with the normal approximation, is applied to the 50 values $D_{c,k}$.

## A3. Supplementary statistical comparisons

\applabel{A3}{app:supp-comparisons}Below are the pairwise test results and two figures behind results stated in the body of this chapter.

**Pairwise tests under queen contiguity.** With SRS as a seventh member, the four pairs that Nemenyi comparisons did not separate were Balanced Quartiles against SRS ($p = 1.00$), $2\times2$ Blocking against High Incidence Focus ($p = 0.32$) and Checkerboard ($p = 0.39$), and Checkerboard against High Incidence Focus ($p = 1.00$). Over the 50 independent configuration-by-surface units, the mean paired differences in MSE between designs adjacent in the six-design mean-MSE order, with $t_{49}$ 95\% intervals, were $-0.0401$ ($-0.0431$, $-0.0372$) for Incidence-Guided Saturation against Balanced Quartiles, $-0.0293$ ($-0.0332$, $-0.0255$) for Balanced Quartiles against Isolation Buffer, $-0.0853$ ($-0.0954$, $-0.0752$) for Isolation Buffer against High Incidence Focus, $-0.0738$ ($-0.0858$, $-0.0617$) for High Incidence Focus against $2\times2$ Blocking, and $-0.7677$ ($-0.7893$, $-0.7460$) for $2\times2$ Blocking against Checkerboard, with Wilcoxon $p \le 4.9\times10^{-9}$ in every case. The better design of each pair had the lower MSE in all 50 units, except High Incidence Focus against $2\times2$ Blocking, where it did so in 48 (96\%). This test follows the mean-MSE order, and it separated High Incidence Focus from $2\times2$ Blocking where the Nemenyi comparison of within-block ranks did not. It did so because each unit's MSE averages over both spillover regimes, and in that average the control-only losses of $2\times2$ Blocking outweigh its both-arms wins.

**Pairwise tests under rook contiguity.** Nemenyi comparisons, with SRS as a seventh member, separated 17 of 21 pairs. The four they did not separate were Incidence-Guided Saturation against Balanced Quartiles ($p = 0.66$) and SRS ($p = 0.14$), Balanced Quartiles against SRS ($p = 0.97$), and $2\times2$ Blocking against Isolation Buffer ($p = 1.00$). Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon tests separated every pair except $2\times2$ Blocking against Isolation Buffer and Balanced Quartiles against SRS (both $p = 0.21$). In the surface-level comparison, Incidence-Guided Saturation had a lower MSE than Balanced Quartiles in 48 of the 50 units (mean difference $-0.0121$; $-0.0139$, $-0.0102$; Wilcoxon $p = 9.9\times10^{-10}$). $2\times2$ Blocking and Isolation Buffer were close: $2\times2$ Blocking had the lower MSE in 36 of the 50 units (72\%; mean difference $-0.0048$; $-0.0078$, $-0.0017$; Wilcoxon $p = 0.0027$). Isolation Buffer, however, had the slightly better average rank (4.21 against 4.33), and the two designs traded places in mean MSE at $\tau = 3$. Every other adjacent pair differed in all 50 units. Within single incidence configurations, rook coverage was between 0.944 and 0.954 for every design except Checkerboard, whose coverage was between 0.155 and 0.165.

## A7. Technical notes

\applabel{A7}{app:technical}

\applabel{A7}{app:technical-notes}This section explains two results reported in the body of this chapter: the bias of Incidence-Guided Saturation grows with $\tau$, and so does the coverage of Checkerboard under rook contiguity. It closes with block-level detail for the results across $\tau$. The stored results keep neither $\hat\rho$ nor the standard error of each fit, so we re-ran every block for the six designs, both neighbor types, and all five values of $\tau$, 2.4 million fits of the oracle model, recording $\hat\rho$ and the standard error. The re-run reproduced the stored results in all 9,600 scenarios. Numbers below that involve $\hat\rho$, the standard error, or the terms of Equation \ref{eq:error-decomposition} come from this re-run. The others come from the stored results.

### Identification diagnostics

Two combinations of design and neighbor type weaken or remove the information that separates $\tau$ from the spillover term. Under rook contiguity, Checkerboard gives $WZ = 1 - Z$ exactly, because every neighbor of a treated cluster is a control and every neighbor of a control is treated. Both spillover covariates then equal $\gamma(1 - Z)$, a linear combination of the intercept and $Z$, so $\tau$ is not identified: the fitting routine drops the aliased spillover column, and the coefficient on $Z$ estimates $\tau - \gamma$. Chapter 2 noted the same consequence of exact collinearity between treatment and spillover exposure, $\hat\beta \approx \beta - \psi$ in its notation. The non-oracle model has no spillover column to drop, but its Checkerboard estimates under rook contiguity have the same defect. Under queen contiguity, each of the 64 interior clusters has four treated and four control neighbors, so $WZ = 1/2$ at every interior cluster. Under the control-only regime the spillover covariate then equals $(\gamma/2)(1 - Z)$ at those clusters, a linear combination of the intercept and $Z$, and only the 36 clusters on the grid boundary carry information that separates it from the intercept and $Z$. As a result, $\tau$ is identified, but imprecisely. In the both-arms regime, the spillover covariate is the constant $\gamma/2$ at interior clusters, confounded with the intercept but not with $Z$. Isolation Buffer under rook contiguity can also, rarely, draw exactly the checkerboard pattern, a maximal independent set that equals one color class of the grid. This happened in 4 of its 40,000 rook draws and affected one fit in each of 20 scenarios, 4 at each value of $\tau$. We flag every fit in which the fitting routine reports an aliased column and every scenario in which some draw has $\text{rank}([1, Z, WZ]) < 3$. Aliased estimates are kept in all summaries. In the exhibits, we flag Checkerboard under rook contiguity, where every fit is aliased. The Isolation Buffer scenarios, each with one aliased fit among its 250, are noted here and carry no flag in the exhibits.


### Estimation error and its dependence on $\tau$

For one fit $(k, j)$, write $Y$, $Z$, and $\epsilon$ for $Y_{kj}$, $Z_{kj}$, and $\epsilon_{kj}$ (Simulation design, resampling, and metrics). Let $V = [1, Z, S(Z), X_k]$ be the $100 \times 4$ covariate matrix of the oracle model, so that Equation \ref{eq:outcome} reads $(I - \rho W)Y = V\theta + \epsilon$ with $\theta = (0, \tau, 1, \beta)^\top$. Let $A = (I - \rho W)^{-1}$ and $V^{+} = (V^\top V)^{-1}V^\top$, and for a vector $v$ write $[V^{+}v]_Z$ for the coefficient on $Z$ when $v$ is regressed on the columns of $V$ by least squares. Given $\hat\rho$, the estimated coefficients are $V^{+}(I - \hat\rho W)Y$ (Estimation and performance criteria). Because $(I - \hat\rho W)Y = V\theta + \epsilon + (\rho - \hat\rho)WY$ and $WY = WA(V\theta + \epsilon)$,
\begin{equation}
\hat\tau - \tau = [V^{+}\epsilon]_Z + (\rho - \hat\rho)\,h + \tau(\rho - \hat\rho)\,g,
\label{eq:error-decomposition}
\end{equation}
where
$$
g = [V^{+}WAZ]_Z, \qquad h = [V^{+}WA\{S(Z) + \beta X_k + \epsilon\}]_Z.
$$
The first term has mean zero given $Z$ and $X_k$. The last term carries a factor of $\tau$. It is present exactly when $g \neq 0$, where $g$ is the coefficient on $Z$ when the lagged treatment $WAZ = WZ + \rho W^2 Z + \rho^2 W^3 Z + \cdots$ is regressed on the model's own covariates. The sign and size of the last term are set by the error in $\hat\rho$. The concentrated likelihood depends on $Y$ only through the residual sum of squares of $(I - \tilde\rho W)Y$ on $V$, and the part of that residual that involves $\tau$ is $\tau(\rho - \tilde\rho)$ times the residual of $WAZ$ on $V$. If $WAZ$ lies in the column space of $V$, that part vanishes for every $\tilde\rho$, so $\hat\rho$ is the same at every value of $\tau$. If, in addition, $g = 0$, then $\hat\tau - \tau$ is the same at every value of $\tau$. Equation \ref{eq:error-decomposition} held on every re-run fit, with a largest residual of $4.2\times10^{-13}$. For Checkerboard under rook contiguity, it held in the reduced form given below.

Two consequences of Equation \ref{eq:error-decomposition} explain the results for $\tau$ reported in the body.

First, for designs whose treated clusters have treated neighbors, the last term gives a small positive bias that grows with $\tau$. Under queen contiguity, pooled over the 160 blocks, the bias of Incidence-Guided Saturation rose from 0.029 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.047 at $\tau = 3$ (Stability across treatment effect sizes), while that of Isolation Buffer stayed between 0.002 and 0.004. Almost all of the rise comes from the last term of Equation \ref{eq:error-decomposition}. In our fits, $\hat\rho$ was biased downward by about 0.06 on average (for Incidence-Guided Saturation, by 0.071 at $\tau = 0.8$ and 0.054 at $\tau = 3$). We observed this downward bias in these simulations but did not derive it or check it against a published finite-sample result. With $\rho - \hat\rho$ positive on average, the last term is positive and grows with $\tau$ for any design with $g > 0$. For Incidence-Guided Saturation, $g$ averaged 0.371 over the queen fits, and the last term contributed 0.021 of the bias at $\tau = 0.8$ and 0.043 at $\tau = 3$. The first term contributed 0.001 at both values, and the second 0.007 and 0.002. For Isolation Buffer, $g$ averaged 0.020, and the last term contributed 0.001 and 0.004. Most of the difference in $g$ comes from the control-only regime. Under the both-arms regime with $\rho = 0$, the lagged treatment is $WZ = S(Z)/\gamma$, one of the covariates, so $g = 0$ for every design. Under the control-only regime, $WZ = S(Z)/\gamma + Z \circ WZ$, and at $\rho = 0$, $g$ is close to the average share of treated neighbors among treated clusters. That share is 0.57 for Incidence-Guided Saturation, whose treated clusters are concentrated in the high-saturation quadrants, and exactly 0 for Isolation Buffer, whose treated clusters have no treated neighbors. For Isolation Buffer, $Z \circ WZ = 0$, so the two regimes define the same spillover covariate and the same $g$, which is 0 at $\rho = 0$ and about 0.06 at $\rho = 0.5$. At $\rho = 0$, its $\hat\rho$ and its estimation error were the same at every value of $\tau$, up to the optimizer's tolerance.

The same term explains why the control-only MSE of Incidence-Guided Saturation rose from 0.131 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.182 at $\tau = 3$ while that of Isolation Buffer did not. Under that regime, averaged over the 80 queen blocks, the variance of the last term of Equation \ref{eq:error-decomposition} rose from 0.008 to 0.061 for Incidence-Guided Saturation, while the variance of the rest of the error changed little (0.119 and 0.115). The variance of the last term grew more slowly than $\tau^2$ because $\hat\rho$ became less variable as $\tau$ grew. For Isolation Buffer, the variance of the last term stayed below 0.0002. The rise in bias slowed at larger values of $\tau$ for a related reason: the part of the likelihood that involves $\tau$ sharpens the likelihood around the true $\rho$ as $\tau$ grows, so the downward bias of $\hat\rho$ shrank.

Second, the decomposition explains why the coverage of Checkerboard under rook contiguity rose with $\tau$, from 0.150 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.464 at $\tau = 3$ (Stability across treatment effect sizes), although its coefficient on $Z$ estimates $\tau - \gamma$ at every value of $\tau$. For this design $WZ = 1 - Z$, and because $W$ is row-standardized, $W^2 Z = W(1 - Z) = Z$. The powers of $W$ applied to $Z$ therefore alternate between $1 - Z$ and $Z$, and $WAZ = \{(1 - Z) + \rho Z\}/(1 - \rho^2)$ lies in the span of the intercept and $Z$. The derivation of Equation \ref{eq:error-decomposition} applies with the aliased spillover column dropped, $V = [1, Z, X_k]$ and $\theta = (\gamma, \tau - \gamma, \beta)^\top$, so that $\tau - \gamma$ takes the place of $\tau$, and $g = -1/(1 + \rho)$. Two consequences follow: $\hat\rho$ is the same at every value of $\tau$, and
$$
\hat\tau - \tau = -\gamma + \delta + (\tau - \gamma)\,\frac{\hat\rho - \rho}{1 + \rho},
$$
where $\delta$ collects the first two terms of that decomposition and, like $\hat\rho$, does not depend on $\tau$. The error in $\hat\rho$ is therefore multiplied by $\tau - \gamma$, which grows with $\tau$. The mean standard deviation of $\hat\tau$ rose from 0.202 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.327 at $\tau = 3$, and the standard error tracked it, rising on average from 0.199 to 0.322. With the bias held near $-\gamma$, wider intervals covered $\tau$ more often. The rise was largest at $\rho = 0$ (coverage 0.157 to 0.562) and smallest at $\rho = 0.5$ (0.142 to 0.284), consistent with the factor $1/(1 + \rho)$. The same term raised the MSE from 0.477 to 0.567. About three quarters of that increase was variance, $(n-1)\text{SD}^2/n$ averaged over scenarios (Appendix \ref{app:mechanics}), which rose from 0.041 to 0.109. The other quarter was squared bias, which rose from 0.436 to 0.458 because $\hat\rho$ was biased slightly downward, moving the mean bias from $-0.650$ to $-0.667$. The higher coverage at large $\tau$ reflects wider intervals around the wrong quantity, not a recovery of $\tau$.

**Block-level detail.** Under queen contiguity, the average rank of Incidence-Guided Saturation among the six designs rose from 1.41 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 1.85 at $\tau = 3$, while that of Balanced Quartiles stayed between 2.13 and 2.14 and that of Isolation Buffer fell from 3.71 to 3.31. Incidence-Guided Saturation had a lower MSE than Balanced Quartiles in 103, 102, 102, 102, and 101 of the 160 blocks at $\tau = 0.8$, 1, 1.5, 2, and 3, and a lower MSE than Isolation Buffer in 75, 73, 56, 40, and 12 of the 80 control-only blocks. Its worst case across blocks was the lowest of the six designs at $\tau \le 1.5$, but at $\tau = 2$ and $\tau = 3$ that of Isolation Buffer was lower (0.207 against 0.210, and 0.208 against 0.238). Under rook contiguity, at $\tau = 3$, Incidence-Guided Saturation had a lower MSE than Isolation Buffer in 47 of the 80 control-only blocks, and its worst case across rook blocks was the lowest of the six designs at every value of $\tau$ except $\tau = 3$, where that of Isolation Buffer was lower (0.173 against 0.174). The coverage of rook Checkerboard was 0.150, 0.162, 0.212, 0.286, and 0.464 at $\tau = 0.8$, 1, 1.5, 2, and 3.

## A8. Observed-incidence application detail

\applabel{A8}{app:nc}The primary application numbers come from the aggregate performance and allocation-risk summaries of the main run and of the separate tail refinement. Annual tables average the six queen parameter pairs equally, without pooled Monte Carlo intervals. Each random draw used a fixed, reproducible seed. An independent check recomputed performance from the stored fits and verified the annual treatment budgets, the regional orderings, and the allocations and outcomes reused from the main run in the tail refinement. The county death-certificate source data are restricted and not publicly available. We report only 58-cluster summaries.

For randomized designs, the prespecified refinement schedule allowed $J=100,200,400$ and $R=100,200,400,1000,2000,4000$. Whichever source of Monte Carlo error, allocations or outcomes, contributed more to the shortfall from the precision targets was extended. All randomized designs met the targets at $J=100$ and $R=100$. For designs with a single possible assignment, only outcomes were extended. If an allocation occurs $n_a$ times among $J$ draws, its risk estimate enters the mean with weight $n_a/J$. The variance due to outcome noise therefore involves squared weights $(n_a/J)^2$, not $n_a/J^2$ as if duplicate estimates were independent. Bias and coverage use the same accounting of frequencies and covariances. The overall precision includes both variation across assignments and outcome noise given an assignment. A design whose sampled assignments happened to coincide is distinguished from one with only one possible assignment. Approximate Monte Carlo standard errors of setting-specific differences between designs treat the designs' random draws as independent, whereas averages across settings or models do not assume that shared allocations are independent. Settings with the same set of possible assignments shared their simulations, with annual treatment counts and population shares recalculated.

We report the estimated variance of risk both raw and with the contribution of outcome Monte Carlo noise subtracted. Signed corrected estimates are retained rather than silently truncated. None is negative in the NC refinement. Quantiles and worst-decile means use noisy estimated conditional risks. To avoid selection bias, worst-decile assignments were identified with one half of the simulated outcomes and evaluated with the other half, and the roles of the two halves were then reversed. The Jaccard overlap of the two worst deciles describes sampled tail membership, not a confidence interval or population tail probability. For a design with only one possible assignment, an overlap of one is uninformative.

**Design adaptations.** Before simulation, we checked the 58-cluster row-standardized contiguity matrix $W$, its binary adjacency and its row order against the boundary geometry. On the NC map, Checkerboard visits clusters by decreasing degree, chooses the arm that conflicts least with assigned neighbors, breaks equal conflicts toward control, and complements the assignment if more than half are treated. In Balanced Quartiles and Balanced Halves, odd-size strata receive their necessary extra treatments at random. In Balanced Halves, one half receives 14 treatments and the other 15, with the extra-treatment half chosen randomly. The four-region partition used by both saturation designs was selected from 250 candidates generated by a geographic $k$-means procedure, by compactness and balance in reference population, cluster count and county count, without consulting outcomes. Reference population is pooled person-years divided by four. Incidence-Guided Saturation first ranks clusters by annual per-capita rates, averages their ranks equally within each region, ranks those four means, and assigns 80/60/40/20\% from highest to lowest. Regional ties are broken randomly per allocation, and local treatment counts are rounded under the retained design rules. Per-capita cluster rates already account for population size. Regional mean ranks weight clusters equally, whereas pooled regional rates, deaths divided by population, weight larger clusters more heavily. Mean raw rates and pooled regional rates are evaluated as prespecified sensitivities rather than chosen by performance. The grid rule averages $X$ directly. Mean ranks align with its rank-scaled Poisson cases but are a deliberate adaptation for the application, not the exact rule used for continuous grid incidence. The 14 groups used by $2\times2$ Blocking are formed once per year by $k$-means on standardized projected coordinates, incidence ranks and log(1+population), then held fixed. Half of each group, rounded, is treated at random, and the single-cluster group of each year remains control, because half of one cluster rounds to zero. The groups are not literal square blocks.

The fixed regional criterion is $C=3s_P+1.5s_K+1.5s_D+c/d_{\max}$, where $s_P$, $s_K$ and $s_D$ are the standard deviations of regional population, cluster and county shares. Here $c$ averages within-region distances to regional centers and $d_{\max}$ is the maximum pairwise distance between the projected cluster coordinates. Candidates use standardized projected coordinates and are selected without outcome performance. The fixed groups used by $2\times2$ Blocking contain one to eight clusters. Yearly total treatments are 28, 31, 27 and 29. Table \ref{tab:nc-order} gives the regional ordering under the primary and alternative summaries, recorded before performance was evaluated.

## A9. Participation, power and sensitivity analyses for the NC application

\applabel{A9}{app:nc-ext}Here we give the detail behind Colleges needed under partial participation and the sensitivity analyses of the application. All numbers come from aggregate summaries of runs that wrote to their own output folders, each with a manifest of parameters, code hashes and package versions. These runs left the production application files unchanged. Unless stated otherwise, results use random volunteering, $\beta = 0$, $\kappa = 0.8$ and the corrected $t$ test, and they average the four planning years.

Results at $\rho = 0$ differed from those at $\rho = 0.5$ by about two colleges or fewer. **Interval calibration.** We tried several corrections and adopted a method only if its coverage lay between 94.0\% and 96.0\% for every design and regime. On the stored fits of the main application ($\beta = 0$), the Wald interval covered 92.6\% to 93.6\% by design and regime. A $t$ reference distribution alone gave 93.2\% to 94.1\%, a degrees-of-freedom-corrected standard error alone 93.5\% to 94.4\%, and the two together 94.1\% to 94.9\%. In a separate run of 500 fits per setting at 58 colleges, parametric percentile bootstrap intervals with 499 replicates covered 90.1\% to 93.6\%, parametric bootstrap-$t$ intervals 93.2\% to 95.8\% and profile-likelihood intervals 91.8\% to 94.7\%. Only the $t$ interval with the corrected standard error met the rule on the stored fits. In the separate 500-fit run it covered 92.8\% to 95.8\% and narrowly missed the rule there, which every other method also missed. Table \ref{tab:nc-calibration} shows its size and coverage at each number of participating colleges. Table \ref{tab:interval-comparison} compares the Wald and corrected intervals for each design in the grid study and the main application.

**Guidance under partial participation.** Table \ref{tab:nc-guidance} gives each strategy's mean MSE relative to SRS at $\tau = 1$ for 20, 29, 40 and 58 participating colleges. When colleges with higher incidence were more likely to volunteer, the ratios at 20 and 29 colleges were within 0.02 of 1 for both saturation designs and Balanced Quartiles under either regime, and within 0.03 for Balanced Halves. Checkerboard and Isolation Buffer remained the worst designs. The four saturation regions were rebuilt on the participants with at least two colleges required in every region. Before that requirement was imposed, a region with fewer than two colleges occurred in 1 of the 50 random subsets at 15 colleges and in one incidence-weighted subset at 20 colleges. Imposing it changed the regions of only two distinct participant subsets and changed no ratio in Table \ref{tab:nc-guidance} by more than 0.01.

**Targeting.** With all 58 colleges, Incidence-Guided Saturation's mean share of the summed college incidence rates in treated colleges was 51.1\%, against 50.4\% for Saturation Quadrants, 50.0\% for SRS and 62.2\% for High Incidence Focus. Its mean share of deaths was 49.2\%, against 49.6\%, 49.7\% and 35.4\%. On the grid, the gain of Incidence-Guided Saturation over Saturation Quadrants in treated incidence share averaged 2.1 to 3.1 percentage points across the five incidence configurations, while the treated incidence share of High Incidence Focus itself reached 0.75 to 0.77 by giving up randomization over the whole map. Grid clusters have equal populations, so rate share and death share coincide there. Figure \ref{fig:spread-gain} shows that the gain rose almost linearly with the spread of the regions' mean incidence ranks, and that the NC regions lie at the low end of that spread.

**Formal tests on the NC results.** Friedman tests over the 24 combinations of year, $\rho$ and $\gamma$ rejected equal ranks of the nine strategies in all four combinations of regime and $\beta$ ($\chi^2 = 135.3$, 153.8, 150.7 and 179.8 on 8 degrees of freedom, $p \le 2.3\times10^{-25}$; Nemenyi critical difference 2.45). Under control-only spillover, Saturation Quadrants and Incidence-Guided Saturation had the two best average ranks (1.67 and 1.79 with $\beta = 0$; 1.29 and 1.71 with $\beta = 1$), and SRS ranked seventh with $\beta = 0$ and sixth with $\beta = 1$. Under both-arms spillover with $\beta = 0$, High Incidence Focus ranked first (1.88) and SRS sixth (5.17), with the balancing and saturation designs between them. These tests treat the 24 blocks as independent, although the years share one map and some strategies share their simulations across years. They therefore describe the consistency of the ordering rather than independent evidence.

**Unequal numbers of trained professionals.** With $m$ proportional to college population and averaging 25, and ICC $= 0.05$, power fell by 0.097 on average across designs, settings and effect sizes. For $d = 0.3$ under both-arms spillover, the mean power over the nine strategies fell from 0.59 to 0.46 with 20 colleges and from 0.88 to 0.77 with 58. MSE rose by a factor of 1.24 to 1.84 across designs and settings, and no design gained relative to the others.

**Estimation models.** Every model in the sensitivity analysis has the mean $\mu = \alpha \mathbf{1} + \tau Z + \text{Spill}$ with the proportional spillover covariate of the main analysis, and uses the 58-college queen geography. The spatial lag model of the main analysis is $Y = \rho W Y + \mu + \epsilon$, $\epsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2 I)$. The CAR model is $Y = \mu + u$, $u \sim N\{0, \sigma^2 (I - \lambda S)^{-1}\}$, where $S$ is the symmetric matrix similar to the row-standardized $W$ [@ord_estimation_1975]. We fitted it by maximum likelihood with the `spautolm` function of the R package `spatialreg` [@bivand_r_2022]. For the reverse comparison, data were generated as $Y = \mu + L\epsilon$ with $LL^\top = (I - \rho S)^{-1}$ and the same values of $\rho$ as the spatial lag data. These runs used four years, $\rho \in \{0, 0.2, 0.5\}$, $\gamma \in \{0.5, 0.8\}$, both regimes and the nine strategies, with 500 fits per setting.

The Bayesian CAR model [@leroux_estimation_2000] is $Y_j = \mu_j + \phi_j + e_j$, $e_j \sim N(0, \nu^2)$, with
\begin{equation*}
\phi_j \mid \phi_{-j} \sim N\left(\frac{\lambda \sum_k a_{jk}\phi_k}{\lambda \sum_k a_{jk} + 1 - \lambda},\; \frac{\sigma_\phi^2}{\lambda \sum_k a_{jk} + 1 - \lambda}\right),
\end{equation*}
where $a_{jk}$ is the binary queen adjacency. We used the defaults of the `S.CARleroux` function of the R package `CARBayes` [@lee_carbayes_2013], version 6.1.1: independent $N(0, 10^5)$ priors for the regression coefficients, inverse-gamma(1, 0.01) priors for $\nu^2$ and $\sigma_\phi^2$, and a uniform(0, 1) prior for $\lambda$. Each chain ran 25,000 iterations, discarding the first 5,000 and thinning by 5. At $\rho = 0.5$, where fewer than half the chains converged, we reran the same data with 100,000 iterations, discarding the first 20,000 and thinning by 20. The Bayesian spatial lag model [@lesage_introduction_2009] has the same form as the maximum likelihood model, with the defaults of the `spBreg_lag` function of `spatialreg`, version 1.4.3: a $N(0, 10^{12} I)$ prior for the regression coefficients, the prior $p(\sigma^2) \propto 1/\sigma^2$, a Beta(1.01, 1.01) prior for $\rho$ rescaled to its feasible interval, and 10,000 draws of which the first 2,000 were discarded. Both Bayesian models used four years, $\rho \in \{0, 0.5\}$, $\gamma = 0.8$, both regimes and the nine strategies, with 100 fits per setting (14,400 fits per model), and both were fitted to the same data as the maximum likelihood model. We report the posterior mean of $\tau$ and the 95\% equal-tailed credible interval. A chain was counted as converged when the effective sample size of $\tau$ was at least 400 and the absolute Geweke $z$ statistic [@geweke_evaluating_1992] was below 1.96.

With the longer chains, 83.1\% of the Bayesian CAR chains at $\rho = 0.5$ converged, against 46.2\% for the shorter chains, but 12.5\% still had an absolute Geweke $z$ of at least 1.96, against about 5\% expected by chance. Among converged chains, the Bayesian CAR estimate was biased by $+0.14$ under both-arms spillover and $+0.22$ under control-only spillover, with credible-interval coverage of 90.4\% and 87.7\%, against biases of $+0.02$ and $+0.03$ and Wald coverage of 93.5\% and 93.2\% for maximum likelihood on the same data. Of the Bayesian spatial lag chains, 94.9\% converged. The median effective sample size of $\tau$ was 8,000 (minimum 5,897), and 5.1\% of chains had an absolute Geweke $z$ of at least 1.96. The model's posterior means correlated 0.999 with the maximum likelihood estimates (mean absolute difference 0.017), its bias was at most 0.04 in absolute value in every combination of $\rho$ and regime, and its credible intervals covered 94.6\% to 95.3\% over all chains (94.5\% to 95.3\% over converged chains). The Spearman correlation of its design ordering with that of maximum likelihood averaged 0.96 to 1.00 across the four combinations of $\rho$ and regime (0.83 in the lowest single block), and the best design agreed in every block. Tables \ref{tab:nc-car} and \ref{tab:nc-bayes} give each strategy's MSE relative to SRS under each model.

**Spillover form.** Under the binary form, $S(Z) = \gamma\,\mathbf{1}\{\text{any treated queen neighbor}\}$, times $1 - Z$ under control-only spillover. Under the count form, $S(Z) = (\gamma/\bar d) \times$ (number of treated queen neighbors), where $\bar d = 4.93$ is the mean number of queen neighbors, so a college of average degree with every neighbor treated receives $\gamma$, as under the proportional form. Table \ref{tab:nc-forms} compares the three forms. With the binary form, Isolation Buffer is never identified, because every control has a treated neighbor, and under control-only spillover no strategy was identified in every fit. The saturation designs were identified most often there (in 89.7\% and 91.7\% of fits) and, among identified fits, had MSE 0.70 to 0.71 times that of SRS.
